News.title: Betting shops ‘at heart of community life’ in Burnham’s own constituency, say voters
News.content:
Next

BETTING shops are at the heart of community life in PM Andy Burnham’s own seat — according to voters in his constituency.

They spoke out as bookies across the country blame shop closures on Labour tax hikes.



Pollsters Opinium found more than half the locals in Makerfield, Greater Manchester, believe the outlets made a positive contribution.

And one in four said they had placed a bet in the last year.



The findings come amid fears that another tax raid on gambling firms could hammer high streets and cost thousands of jobs.

Industry modelling claims higher Machine Games Duty could lead to as many as 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casinos shutting their doors and almost 16,000 job losses.



Betting and Gaming Council Chief Executive Grainne Hurst said: “Makerfield tells a very human story about what betting shops mean to communities across Britain.

“The Prime Minister has said policies should face a ‘Makerfield test’ that if they don’t work for people here and don’t lift them up, they shouldn’t happen at all.”

Mr Burnham used the “Makerfield test” after winning the seat, saying policies that do not work for people in the constituency or “lift people up” should not happen.

Betfred founder Fred Done has also warned that further gambling tax rises in the upcoming Budget could devastate the high street betting industry.



The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign is urging ministers not to hike betting duties at the Budget.

Chancellor John Healey will reveal his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, 28 October.

News.title: British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken
News.content:
FAST AND LOOS British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken







Next

BRITISH Airways is keeping a Boeing 777 flying — even though almost half its toilets are broken.

Passengers are having to queue for the loo at 30,000ft because four washrooms are locked.



Only two are working for the 84 First and Club passengers while the 170 in World Traveller class have to share three.

The plane, which does regular 11-hour flights from Heathrow to ­worldwide destinations including the US and India, also has no wifi.



In the next few days it has been scheduled to fly to and from the UK, New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

Passengers are not told of the problems before booking flights but get a scripted apology on landing.

One crew member said: “It’s unacceptable.

“Why are we hoodwinking passengers this way?”

Another said: “Staff are in the frontline of passengers’ upset at having splashed out on premium fares only to be offered a service that you’d be disgusted to experience on a cheap, no-frills’ carrier.”

BA said it had apologised to affected customers and “offered a gesture to help put things right”.



Sources said it hopes to repair the problem plane “in the next few days”.

News.title: Labour’s hated ‘holiday tax’ risks turning London into a tourism ‘ghost town’, top Tory warns
News.content:
Next

A PUNISHING holiday tax risks turning London into a tourism “ghost town”, a senior Tory says.

It could jeopardise the capital’s economic success if implemented by the Labour mayor Sadiq Khan.



The warning comes from Tory mayoral hopeful Sir James Cleverly after he put himself forward for the job.

He said: “I want to make sure that London is buzzing, London is vibrant, London’s attracting people, London’s contributing to the UK economy.



“The last thing we need is anything that would put that at risk, anything that would turn London into a ghost town.”

More than 20million foreign tourists visited London last year, contributing £40billion, he claimed.

He also said the PM’s “anti-London policies” were hurting the South.

The Sun has launched a Hands Off Our Hols campaign, warning it will price hard-working families out of staycations.



England’s local leaders are to get the power to introduce a fee per overnight stay.

Labour’s 10 regional mayors in England have committed to bringing in the visitor levy, but two Tory and two Reform mayors ruled out implementing the measure which could damage a city’s nightlife.

Mr Khan is enthusiastically pushing for the tourist tax to be charged at up to five per cent of the cost of a hotel room.

Trade body UKHospitality has warned it could add £100 to a family holiday.

Mr Cleverly quit Kemi Badenoch‘s top team to throw his weight behind running for London mayor.



If successful, he would be the first Tory to win the capital since Boris Johnson in 2012.

News.title: Jill Dando cops launch new probe into unsolved murder as hope CCTV could prove answers on mystery man
News.content:
Next

COPS have launched a fresh probe into the shocking unsolved murder of the adored TV star Jill Dando.

Detectives are re-examining CCTV of a mystery man who they believe could hold the key to cracking the 27-year-old case.



The Met is now using modern technology to enhance original footage from Putney Bridge Tube station, reports The Mirror.

It shows an unidentified man spotted around a mile from Jill’s Fulham home shortly after she was callously shot on her doorstep.



The force said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando‘s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.

“This remains ongoing.”

The man, known as Man X, was filmed around 20 minutes after Jill was shot outside her home in Gowan Avenue, South West London, on April 26, 1999.



Cold-case officers are understood to have spent the past ten months finding and digitising the original footage.

It was believed to be buried among 223 boxes of material in police storage.

Now detectives hope clearer images could help establish who Man X was — and whether he was linked to the killing.

The footage is also being examined for possible links to Milorad Ulemek, a notorious Serbian paramilitary commander known as Legija.

Ulemek, a former French Foreign Legionnaire, led a unit involved in assassinations during the rule of former Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic.



A facial comparison expert previously identified similarities between Ulemek and Man X.

He said they had similar mouths, chins, hairlines and right sideburns.

Their noses and right ears were also said to be similar in shape and size.



A dent on Ulemek’s nose was also highlighted as matching one shown on a police e-fit released after Jill’s murder.

Two key witnesses have also said Ulemek resembled men they saw near the murder scene.

One woman was driving along Fulham Palace Road when she saw a man in a suit “running for his life”.

A month later, she picked out Man X in CCTV as the man she had seen.

But detectives dismissed her evidence, saying her original description did not match Man X.



Both men, however, were said to have been wearing suits and ties and had similar heights, builds and hair colour.

Jill’s neighbour Richard Hughes saw the gunman and believed he may have been carrying a mobile phone.

He said the killer “looked like” an e-fit produced by the female witness.

Another neighbour, Geoffrey Upfillbrown, also saw the killer and said the image looked “similar”, according to police notes.

A second key witness later said he was “80%” sure the man he saw near the scene was Ulemek.



Jill, 37, was ambushed from behind as she approached her front door.

She was killed instantly by a single bullet to her left temple.

At the time, Britain was bombing Serbia and Jill was one of the country’s best-known TV presenters.

She had fronted BBC shows including Crimewatch and Holiday.

Within hours of her murder, the BBC received a call claiming it was linked to a NATO attack on a Belgrade TV station.



There were also fears Jill had been targeted because she fronted a BBC appeal for Kosovan refugees 20 days before her death.

Nearly a year later, detectives focused on local man Barry George.

George, now 65, spent eight years behind bars after being convicted of Jill’s murder.

He was cleared at a retrial in 2008.

The case was moved to “inactive” in 2015 following a forensic review.



Ulemek is serving a 40-year sentence in Serbia after being convicted of helping to plan the assassinations of former Serbian president Ivan Stambolic in 2000 and prime minister Zoran Djindjic in 2003.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

George is currently facing trial over historical sex charges.

The Met investigation into Jill’s murder remains ongoing.

News.title: Afghan asylum seeker masterminded  crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK
News.content:
PRISON CALLING Afghan asylum seeker masterminded crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK







Next

AN AFGHAN asylum seeker masterminded a crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK, a court heard yesterday.

Amir Khadikhel, his fellow Afghan Ismat Miakhel and Indian Mansoor Mohammed sent more than 62,000 to the Far East and Middle East using unwitting courier firms DHL and UPS.



The operation was uncovered ­following a tip-off from a victim who used the Find My Phone app to trace hers to a warehouse at Heathrow Airport.

A police raid recovered 3,000 stolen mobiles.



Suspects were later seen handing over phones and wads of cash outside a shop in North London.

A search of a London property led to phones being found under a hidden trapdoor and a further swoop recovered 299 more when some were heard ringing in sealed boxes.

Southwark crown court heard the phones had been stolen across the country.

They can be worth up to £3,700 in China because, unlike new phones, they are not subject to government restrictions.



Khadikhel’s lawyer said he came to the UK after fleeing Afghanistan in 2019, leaving behind his wife and child.

He said he was homeless and had mental health issues, and was lured into criminality by a person who housed him.

Khadikhel and Mohammed both admitted conspiring to receive ­stolen mobile phones, as well as participating in the criminal activities of an organised crime group.

Khadikhel also admitted conspiring to transfer the phones out of the UK.

Miakhel earlier admitted conspiring to receive and transfers stolen goods. Khadikhel, 35, of Wanstead, was jailed for 9½ years.



Miakhel, 33, of Walthamstow, got nine years and Mohammed, 30, of Wood Green, six years and five months.

News.title: Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STAB DENIAL Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green







Next

A MAN yesterday denied the attempted murder of two Jewish men who were stabbed in Golders Green.

Essa Suleiman, 45, also pleaded not guilty to attacking another man earlier the same day.

The case is no longer being treated as terrorism and Suleiman is currently being detained in Broadmoor secure psychiatric hospital, the Old Bailey heard.



Suleiman, of Camberwell, South London, is also accused of one count of possession of a bladed article in a public place following a series of attacks on April 29.



At 8.50am that day, a suspect armed with a knife arrived at an address in Great Dover Street, South London.

Ishmail Hussein received minor injuries and police carried out inquiries at an address connected to Suleiman.

Later that morning, he allegedly attacked two Jewish men in Golders Green, North London.

Shloime Rand, 34, and Norman Shine, 76, both received stab wounds.

Suleiman, a British national born in Somalia, appeared via videolink from Broadmoor hospital and spoke only to confirm his identity.

The case was adjourned for psychiatric reports and a three-week trial is due to go ahead from March 1.

The next hearing is due to be held on January 15.

News.title: Woman ‘raped by unknown man’ in city centre alleyway as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to
News.content:
'ATTACK' HORROR Woman ‘raped by unknown man’ in city centre alleyway as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to







Next

A WOMAN was allegedly raped by an unknown man in a city centre alleyway.

Cops have now released a CCTV image of a person they wish to speak following the shocking attack in Staffordshire earlier this year.



Officers said a woman was approached by an “unknown man” near Bucknall Old Road in Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent at around 1pm on May 11.

The woman was then taken to an alleyway where she was raped, police said.



Staffordshire Police has now released CCTV of a man they believe can help them in their investigation.

A force spokesperson said: “Detectives have been carrying out a number of enquiries as part of an ongoing investigation and are now able to release an image of a man we want to speak to.”



Any witnesses or anyone with information is urged to contact the police quoting incident 457 of May 11.

News.title: Supporters of WASPI compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one, study shows
News.content:
Supporters of WASPI compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one, study shows

EXCLUSIVE: More than 3.5 million women born in the 1950s lost out after the Department for Work and Pensions increased the State Pension age from 60 to 66 but did not properly inform those affected

View 3 Images Around half (47%) of voters believe women affected by State Pension age changes should receive full or partial redress (Image: Leon Neal, Getty Images)

Supporters of compensation for WASPI (Women Against State Pension Inequality) women outnumber opponents by almost four to one, according to a new analysis of more than 10,000 voters.

‌



Around half (47%) of voters believe women affected by State Pension age changes should receive full or partial redress, the Stack Data Strategy research showed. Just 13% believe the women were not wronged or should not be compensated.

‌



More than 3.5 million women born in the 1950s lost out after the Department for Work and Pensions increased the State Pension age from 60 to 66 but did not properly inform those affected.

‌



Keir Starmer’s government refused to roll out a compensation package, as recommended by an independent ombudsman back in 2024. But campaigners have been given new hope after Andy Burnham agreed to meet with them to discuss putting the scandal right, the Mirror reported in July.

WASPI new hope as Andy Burnham set to meet campaign over redress options READ MORE :

WASPI campaign sets out next steps after judicial review challenge launched READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham has agreed to meet with campaigners to discuss putting the scandal right (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

When presented with the Parliamentary Ombudsman's ruling and asked to choose between a range of options for how the Government could respond, more than eight in ten (83%) chose an option involving some form of financial compensation.

‌



The most popular options were paying the maximum compensation recommended and paying proportionate amounts of between £1,000 and £2,950 per woman.

In the Prime Minister’s own constituency of Makerfield in Greater Manchester, 48% of voters back compensation, while just 12%are against payouts.

‌



More than a third (37%) of respondents say the new Labour leader refusing to compensate WASPI women would make them less likely to vote for the party at the next election. Of 2024 Labour voters, a similar number (38%) believe they would be less likely to stick with the party if compensation was refused.

View 3 Images Angela Madden , chair of the WASPI campaign, said the poll sent a clear message to the government (Image: PA)

Angela Madden, chair of the WASPI (Women Against State Pension Inequality) campaign, said: “This research sends a clear message to ministers: supporters of compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one.

‌



“We are pleased that Andy Burnham has recognised the harms experienced by WASPI women and has committed to meeting us to discuss what providing fair redress looks like. WASPI stands ready to work with the Government to identify a solution that is fair to both affected women and the taxpayer.”

A DWP spokesman said: “The Secretary of State set out the Government’s position in his oral statement to Parliament, including acceptance of maladministration and apology to the women affected.

“Our focus now is on delivering an action plan to implement lessons learned in how DWP communicates State Pension matters going forward."

Article continues below

The MRP poll was carried out by Stack Data Strategy between July 8 and August 4 among 10,052 GB adults.

News.title: Oasis 2027 updates: Liam Gallagher argues with fans as thousands scramble for tickets
News.content:
The first of nine sale slots for tickets to Oasis Live '27 has begun as fans up and down the country battle it out to be one of the lucky few who get to see the Gallagher brothers perform live

By the end of the day, there will be some very happy Oasis fans out there. Today is the first of three days in which registered fans will be able to buy tickets for Oasis Live '27, with three limited time slots taking place.

Just two years after their last reunion tour, the Gallagher brothers and their bandmates are coming back to a select group of cities. Naturally, there are millions who want tickets to see their favourite Mancunians perform Wonderwall, Don't Look Back in Anger and Champagne Supernova, but there will also be many left disappointed as they walk away from tough ticket sales without one of the coveted tickets.

Back in 2025, Oasis ticket sales caused swathes of controversy amid queues that lasted hours, site glitches and dynamic pricing. Ticketmaster and Oasis have both said dynamic pricing - the practice of hiking or lowering prices based on demand - will not be used this time.

To deal with the queues, only fans who registered for tickets will be able to join the the ticket queue at one of nine limited slots. There will be three today, three tomorrow and three on Sunday. But some resellers have already started listing their tickets online, despite attempts to prevent this. Some have been listed for more than double the original price and fans have been warned against buying them amid scams and price hikes last year.

Follow along with us as we look at what this means for your ticket chances...

News.title: 'Breakthrough in Jill Dando murder after 27 years brings hope for justice'
News.content:
'Breakthrough in Jill Dando murder after 27 years brings hope for justice'

"A fresh probe will use state-of-the-art technology to look back to the day of the murder. CCTV enhancement could give investigators fresh eyes on the events"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

After nearly three decades, police may be close to a breakthrough in the murder of Jill Dando.

A fresh probe will use state-of-the-art technology to look back to the day of the murder. CCTV enhancement could give investigators fresh eyes on the events.

And after the Mirror's three-year investigation into the senseless crime, we welcome this new development, whatever it uncovers. The original investigation was one of the biggest ever undertaken by the Met. Yet despite thousands of hours of work by dozens of officers, the wrong man was caught and convicted.

After so long, many didn't dare hope a fresh breakthrough with new evidence would be possible. What everyone desperately hopes for is that which has been denied for 27 long years - Justice for Jill.

At the very least, new information could bring some measure of closure and comfort for her family after so many years.

Yvette Cooper's horror at maternity care

We share Yvette Cooper's horror at the deepening crisis in NHS maternity care.

This has been brought into sharp focus by a harrowing and avoidable tragedy. A mum in North Devon had to make her own way to another hospital because her nearest maternity unit is closed - only to be told her baby had died.

The hospital was closed due to being short staffed - but it followed a string of failures in care and communication. But it's far from the only case, and North Devon District is far from the only hospital where patients have been let down.

New mums deserve better than to face giving birth in the back of a car in a lay-by.

Proper standards that can be relied upon by women across the country are long overdue, and it's good that this will be among the first issues she tackles as Health Secretary.

Back to playschool

The BBC are heading back through the round window with a reboot of Playschool - aiming to stave off AI slop aimed at kids. Hopefully someone will wake Big Ted and Little Ted up from their 40-year hibernation.

News.title: Donald Trump 'shelves plans for airstrikes on Mexico' in fight against cartels
News.content:
Donald Trump 'shelves plans for airstrikes on Mexico' in fight against cartels

Relations between the US and Mexico have improved markedly as of late, and Donald Trump is now said to have rowed back on the threat of airstrikes to take out drug cartels

View 3 Images Donald Trump and Claudia Sheinbaum (file) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has reportedly shelved plans to launch airstrikes on Mexico.

‌



The president had suggested the US could conduct strikes in Mexico to tackle drug cartels and immigration at the start of his second term.

‌



However Mexico, so hated by Trump during his first term, has grown closer with its northern neighbour, while Canada is now firmly in America's crosshairs.

‌



Illegal border crossings from Mexico have decreased, and earlier this year US intelligence aided Mexican special forces in capturing Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) leader Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes. Known as El Mencho, he had been the most wanted drug trafficker in the world, but died shortly after his arrest due to wounds he suffered during the prior shootout.

View 3 Images El Mencho was the world's most wanted drug lord (Image: DEA)

Mexico cartel boss El Mencho buried in solid gold coffin as cause of death revealed READ MORE :

Horror as two decapitated human heads found near Sinaloa bank just hours apart READ MORE :

The Trump administration has recently praised Mexico’s efforts to tackle cartels. According to the New York Times, citing US and Mexican officials, Trump has “effectively shelved plans for US airstrikes on Mexican soil” for now.

‌



It comes as a new trade deal between the two countries appears to be on the horizon. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum recently said she and Trump had reached agreements on several key issues following a call, and her US counterpart declared a deal was “very close”.

“I’m very proud to tell you we have a very good relationship with the Mexican government,” Trump told the United Nations on Tuesday. “We’ve made great strides, very great strides with Mexico.”

View 3 Images National Guards patrol the area outside of the General Prosecutor's headquarters in Mexico City following El Mencho's death (Image: AP)

Article continues below

Trump has been ramping up pressure on Mexico to do more about cartels since taking office again, having offered a reward of up to $15m for information that might lead to El Mencho’s capture in December 2024.

The White House designated the CJNG as a foreign terrorist organisation last year. And after El Mencho died, Trump posted on Truth Social: “Mexico must step up their effort on Cartels and Drugs!”

At the time, reports suggested the US provided intelligence for the operation that led to El Mencho’s capture and death, although the extent of this was unclear.

News.title: At least 13 dead as military plane crashes in DR Congo – 'burned beyond recognition'

At least 13 people have been killed following a horrifying plane crash.

‌



The military plane went down in the Democratic ‌Republic of Congo on Friday as it was travelling from Kikwit to the capital, Kinshasa.

‌



Remy Saki Bokinda, vice governor of Kwango province, said the plane experienced a technical problem and attempted ⁠to land in Kenge before crashing in a ball of flames on a "residential plot".

Passengers included the army's auditor general General Likulia Bakumi as well as several other senior military officials. Civilians are also among the dead.

News.title: 'Latest Jill Dando update is a huge development and changes everything for police'
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police's announcement that it is examining CCTV from Putney Bridge tube station is a significant development.

It is the first time in more than two decades that police officers have followed a "new and realistic line of enquiry" in relation to Jill's murder.

And the fact the Met has spoken publicly about "recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology," while specifying they are looking at "original footage from Putney Bridge train station," indicates that they feel they have a strong lead.

Previous police statements have been non-committal but this one is different and is a real change in emphasis. They are now actively looking at the evidence, using the latest technology and even naming the tube station.

View 4 Images Jill Dando (Image: PA)

Man cleared of Jill Dando murder denies raping teenage girl in 1987 READ MORE :

This all comes 12 years after the case was moved to "inactive," meaning it was not being investigated or subject to reviews like most other unsolved murders.

Though Jill's brother, Nigel, has said in the past he hoped her killer might confess, he knew that was unlikely and many who have followed the case believed it would never be solved.

The brutal and apparently inexplicable murder of a 37-year-old woman on her own doorstep in broad daylight on a busy London street would have been shocking enough. But for the victim to be one of the best-known BBC presenters in the UK left the nation united in shock and disbelief.

View 4 Images One of our previous front page stories

The investigation mushroomed into the second biggest homicide probe ever carried out by the Metropolitan Police. Operation Oxborough was under intense pressure from the start.

The Met Police was dealing with the fallout from the Macpherson report that two months earlier branded it "institutionally racist" over Stephen Lawrence's murder (the Met's biggest ever homicide investigation).

It soon became apparent the Jill Dando case would be hard to solve.

Det Chief Insp Hamish Campbell's murder squad interviewed more than 2,500 people, traced 1,200 cars and produced 3,700 exhibits. The £2.75million investigation looked into hundreds of leads.

The team of 45 officers checked 80,000 mobile phones and trawled through hundreds of hours of CCTV.

They analysed 60 firearm murders of women, checked out 8,000 names given to police and traced 20,000 blue Range Rovers.

According to former Met Commissioner Sir John Stevens' 2005 autobiography, 3,000 letters, calls and emails came in each day.

View 4 Images Our first story naming Milorad Ulemek

Barry George was arrested in April 2000 and it took a year to make the case "absolutely watertight", Stevens wrote. He recalled: "The last thing we wanted was another Lawrence-type fiasco."

He said the conviction came as an "immense relief" - but George was acquitted in a 2008 retrial after eight years wrongly spent in prison.

Michael Mansfield KC, who defended him during his first 2001 trial for Jill's murder, argued then that it could have been a Serbian hitman.

Mr Mansfield later said of the Mirror's investigation: "Compelling evidence involved a strong suggestion of Serbian involvement so this is more than a coincidence.

"The Met needs to be monitored closely to ensure they do review this material as the former officer in charge of the case wrongly maintains Barry George’s guilt."

Along with former colleague Matthew Young and many other Mirror staff, I have been investigating the case since November 2023.

Matthew got access to the files from Barry George's 2001 trial and that enabled us to build up a detailed picture of what witnesses saw on the day of the murder.

It was a complex and confusing picture, but at its heart were a number of witnesses who saw a man (or men) in a suit running or sweating in and around the murder scene.

One was a female motorist who told police she had seen a man "running for his life" down the Fulham Palace Road.

The woman later picked out that man in CCTV from Putney Bridge station but detectives rejected her evidence.

Police had originally focused on tracing the running/sweating man and issued an e-fit compiled by one observant witness who stood next to him at a bus stop for a number of minutes.

But after months of dead ends, having never traced the potential suspect, the police pivoted to looking at local men and settled on George.

Now 27 years on, I am hopeful that the killer can be identified and believe the evidence exists to build a strong case against him.

News.title: 'Man City has gaslit its own fans by recklessly claiming innocence over 115 charges - I demand an explanation'
News.content:
"We can all be very calm because not one rule has been broken by Man City."

That's what we were told - or at least that's what the Manchester City top dogs told the players when the 115 charges were announced.

Now, we all look like mugs. Especially those of us that were naive enough to believe them.

For years the loyal City fanbase has heard every possible grumbling from the suits at the Etihad - essentially, this was a witch hunt. 'We're just too good, so they're trying to get us for it'.

‌



Well, congratulations City, you've gaslit your entire fanbase, and the stain of this will live a lot longer than the 48-hour reckless foray into the European Super League.

View 7 Images (L-R) Khaldoon Al Mubarak, former director of football Txiki Begiristain and CEO Ferran Soriano (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

Man City release statement after being found GUILTY of Premier League charges READ MORE :

We've been here before. City fans were not new to it. Two years before the 115 charges were levelled at City by the Premier League, the club successfully overturned a two-year UEFA ban from the Champions League.

It took just five months for the Court of Arbitration for Sport to overturn that ban. Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said the UEFA investigation was a frustrating distraction, but it proved City had done nothing wrong.

‌



It's true. The club had been proved right, and its constant insistence of innocence was vindicated.

So, fast forward two years, and why shouldn't the fans believe them again? After all, the Premier League's 115 charges were based on the exact same leaked dossier that UEFA had used in its own probe.

View 7 Images Soriano and Al Mubarak have a lot of explaining to do to their own fans (Image: VINCE MIGNOTT/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock)

The formula was identical; charges brought, City plead innocence. Except this time, the fans had the precedent to believe them.

‌



Football is incredibly tribal in this country. It's natural that fans back their own club - and equally natural for rival fans to assume guilt.

These 115 charges have been lingering over us fans for three-and-a-half years now. You'd struggle to find a single match in that time when rival fans didn't level the obvious 'we know what you are, we know what you are, you cheating b******s, we know what you are' chant at us.

So tedious. It's instantly responded by cheers and ironic celebrations from City fans. It was boring. So boring.

View 7 Images The club has consistently denied the charges levelled by the Premier League (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

‌



We had to contend with B-rate ex-professionals and boozed up fans calling into phone-in radio shows saying that City will inevitably be relegated out of the Football League at some point soon. Clearly this was nonsense. None of these people had any idea what they were talking about, because the case was heard behind closed doors.

Any sanction could only really result in a points deduction. Even in the worst case scenario for City, it would mean a single relegation to the Championship; this was a case brought by the Premier League specifically, not the FA or the EFL.

But that didn't stop the commentary by rival fans. Guilty. They didn't know a thing... but guilty.

View 7 Images Sanctions won't overshadow the best memories for fans - including reaching 100 points in 2017 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A peak behind the curtain of Man City fans' social media, and we were cautiously optimistic. There's never smoke without fire, but everything we heard from the City camp was a confidence-booster.

Even immediately after the charges were brought in February 2023, the club said it was "surprised", "particularly given the extensive engagement and vast amount of detailed materials that the EPL has been provided with".

There's a vast amount of evidence for our case? Happy days. It even said there was a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" that supports innocence. It doesn't get more confident than that.

Then there was behind-the-scenes chats with the players - who, let's be honest, have the most to lose from relegation.

‌



View 7 Images Loyal fans remained cautiously optimistic about the outcome of the case (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Immediately after the charges were announced, CEO Ferran Soriano and then-sporting director Txiki Begiristain told the entire squad and backroom staff that there was nothing to worry about, according to former defender Aymeric Laporte.

He said: "When I was there and the news broke, the sporting director (Txiki Begiristain) and the CEO (Ferran Soriano) came and told all the players and staff that we can all be very calm because not one rule has been broken by Man City.

"They told us everything was fine so that’s why we all think City will be fine. I don’t think there will be any issues."

‌



View 7 Images The fans will be left heartbroken by any guilty verdicts (Image: Getty Images)

Then there was the chairman himself, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also comes out of this mess looking bad. He's consistently said he can't speak much about the case, but that he'll "say everything I've wanted to say" after the charges were settled.

So here we are, and we're ready to listen... because this is going to take some explaining.

But, despite the bitter taste this sorry charade has left in the mouth, it won't overshadow some of our most-memorable moments. Even if we're playing in the second tier of English football next season, nothing will take away Sergio Aguero's 90+4 finish to seal City's first Premier League title. Neither Ilkay Gundogan's brace to snatch the title away from Liverpool in the dying moments, nor Rodri smashing it home in Istanbul to win the club's first Champions League title. Those memories will be there forever, regardless, and the sorry fans from the days of 'typical City' will be eternally grateful.

‌



But, the club has some serious explaining to do.

News.title: Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

The Athletic , externalis reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count.

The Premier League declined to comment.

Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way.

Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added.

BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings.

Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the independent panel's decision and have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim.

News.title: Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City
News.content:
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.

BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on almost all of the charges.

We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.

But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?

News.title: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
News.content:
E-bikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

Six forces responded to say e-bikes they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

E-bikes have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.

News.title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process".

During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses.

Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind.

An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029.

Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be.

"All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead."

News.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
News.content:
A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.

But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.

It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.

Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.

A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.

A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.

A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.

Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.

And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.

That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.

News.title: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead
News.content:
Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones from the roof and plaza.

In a letter to the Pentagon and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Duckworth said they "must reject this foolhardy plan and instead focus on increasing the safety of the airspace".

The arch is to be built just outside Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, and about 4mi (6km) from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, the site of the deadly 2025 midair crash between a military helicopter and commercial plane.

"The American people cannot afford to stand witness to Trump's risky plan to place a 250-foot (72m) structure along a busy approach path, especially if he follows through on plans to station snipers on the arch and fly drones," Duckworth wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the BBC's US partner, CBS News.

The FAA, however, ruled last week that the massive structure would not pose a risk to flights coming into and out of the airport.

On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, announced it was ending required consultations with local officials about how the structure might affect 42 historic properties in the area.

The council said in the announcement that the National Park Service, which oversees federal landmarks, had proposed a plan for mitigating potential harms to those properties, but local historic preservation officers "raised concerns with the purpose and need of the Triumphal Arch". They also questioned whether the service had adequately identified possible harms and planned sufficient actions to address them.

Federal and state officials are not required to reach an agreement on a project's harm-mitigation plans, and those consultations are allowed to be terminated if both sides can't agree. The council expects to submit a final report on the process early next month.

Meanwhile, Democratic Virginia Congressman Don Beyer says excavation work on the site where the arch will stand has already begun.

Beyer, who is leading congressional opposition to the arch, said he found workers operating heavy equipment when he visited the site on Thursday who told him they were "conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil".

That is "deeply troubling", Beyer said, particularly because the administration is required to give 48 hours notice before work can begin.

"The Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project," Beyer wrote.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

News.title: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside
News.content:
A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain.

The man fell into a gully while descending from the summit of Torrecerredo in the Cantabrian Mountains on Thursday, the Spanish Civil Guard said.

Police and an air unit were deployed to the scene after emergency services were called around 13:27 local time (11:27 GMT). The man's body was recovered by a mountain rescue unit.

The UK Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities "following reports of the death of a British national in Spain".

Spanish emergency services said they initially received a call saying that a person had fallen on the eastern face of the mountain and dispatched a rescue group aboard a medical helicopter.

A doctor among them confirmed the man's death at about 14:18 and remained at the scene to guard the body until a Civil Guard helicopter could arrive about an hour and 20 minutes later.

Specialist mountain rescuers were then lowered by winch to the site of the accident, where they recovered the man's body and belongings.

The identity of the climber, who Spanish authorities said was English, has not been given. The accident occurred when he was about 20 metres from the mountain's summit.

His body has been transported to the Institute of Legal Medicine, which provides forensic pathology services, in Asturias, the Civil Guard said.

Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,650m, is in the Picos de Europa, which is popular with climbers and walkers.

The region's tourism board describes the route up the mountain as "very difficult" with a demanding ascent, warning climbers to take particular care on steep and exposed upper sections on their way down.

Sepa Asturias - the body responsible for emergency services in the region - said it also transported a 54-year-old French woman to hospital after she suffered a leg injury on the mountain range on Thursday afternoon.

News.title: Watch: What could the potential sanctions for Man City be?
News.content: Football finance expert Kieran Maguire says the potential sanctions for Manchester City will be 'significant' after the sources told BBC Sport that the club has been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

News.title: Noah Woods left playground through gap in fence, inquest hears
News.content:
Suffolk Coroner's Court heard from police that Noah had left the playground, walked into a memorial garden and left that through an open gate. He then ran down a path on a new housing estate towards nearby Decoy Pond.

Det Ch Insp Matt Connick from Suffolk Police told the court that CCTV showed Noah in the play area being looked after by a relative, which was "part of a normal routine".

The detective said Noah "left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate".

After he had left the play area, he was closely followed by the relative trying to catch up with him, Connick added.

The inquest heard the relative had shouted out to Noah, who lived in neighbouring East Bergholt, but he went out of sight shortly afterwards.

Another man was said to have joined the search and then police were called.

At the time of the search, volunteers were told that Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf.

A statement from Brantham Parish Council, which maintains the play area at Merriam Close, said it was "deeply saddened by Noah's death and our thoughts remain with his family and all those affected at this extremely difficult time".

"The parish council understands that there was a break in the internal fencing, being constructed to separate the play area from the memorial garden, however the whole of the area at Merriam Close, including the play area and memorial garden are completely enclosed by appropriate perimeter fencing," it said.

"The council will co-operate fully with any investigation and, while inquiries are ongoing, does not consider it appropriate to comment further."

News.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

News.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
News.content:
Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails."

He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity.

"I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans."

He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future.

"We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said.

"Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people."

Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately.

"And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission.

"I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest."

The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One and iPlayer at 09:00 BST on 27 September.

News.title: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
News.content:
NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping.

Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home.

NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches.

The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death.

The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem.

News.title: PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers
News.content:
The prime minister has ruled out handing powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government.

Andy Burnham said other UK nations do not have such powers and he did not "think we can create a different arrangement for Wales".

He added that the decision should be made jointly with Westminster, arguing that the UK Parliament has to have a "say on an issue of that magnitude".

Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said last week he would seek powers to hold an independence referendum, although he ruled out staging one before the next Senedd election in May 2030.

Burnham also said he was open to looking at the Welsh government's "Cynnal" plans to trial offering Â£10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six, in households already receiving universal credit.

This would require the agreement of the Department for Work and Pensions and HMRC to avoid the payment being taxed or other benefits - paid for by the UK government - being reduced.

"I'll certainly ensure that there's a proper discussion about the issue," he said.

"I mean, I did things as mayor of Greater Manchester without there having to be any tax implications.

"So I'm not quite sure why that arises in this in this instance, but we will have a look at it for certain."

News.title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
News.content:
The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day.

In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial.

She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B.

She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse.

In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her.

Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface".

Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die.

The prosecution barrister also outlined further aggravating and mitigating factors.

She said, in sentencing, the youth of the victims had to be taken account, as well as the "multitude of offences", which "spanned a considerable period of time", and the fact there were two victims.

Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years.

"In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said.

"I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with."

Vaughan said he acknowledged the court would impose a "lengthy custodial sentence", but that he had complete confidence that the court would treat Donaldson in the same way it would any other defendant of a similar age and in similar circumstances.

Addressing Donaldson directly, Judge Paul Ramsey said: "Mr Donaldson, I will be sentencing you as soon as I can next month."

News.title: Contentious Orange Order parade can go ahead, commission says
News.content:
The Parades Commission has announced that a planned Orange Order parade is to be allowed on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.

The commission said the parade on Sunday should start earlier than the Orange Order wanted and with fewer people - but can go ahead.

The decision is facing a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposes the march and has said the challenge will be heard on Saturday morning.

Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the commission has said the march can begin at 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested.

As it happened: Parades Commission says Orange Order Drumcree parade can go ahead

In a detailed document known as a determination, which was published on its website, external, the commission said: "This decision is not, and should not be perceived, as a victory for one side or a loss for another.

"It is the outworking of the application of the legal framework to the facts available to the commission."

News.title: PM says bailed sex offender case must be reviewed
News.content:
The prime minister has said that the decision to bail a sex offender and repeatedly allow him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted must be reviewed.

Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them.

Andy Burnham called the case "disturbing", adding: "I would ask those working across the criminal justice system to look at it and to make any necessary changes as a result."

The Ministry of Justice said while the Crown Prosecution Service had the right to challenge them, final bail decisions were "made by the independent judiciary".

The ministry added: "The protection of victims, witnesses, and the public must always be considered when deciding whether or not an offender should be released on bail."

London's victims' commissioner Andrea Simon said victims and their families had been "grossly failed" by the court system that granted Dogan bail.

She said the case showed "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review.

Speaking outside the court where Dogan was jailed, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley criticised the "unfathomable decisions" of the justice system.

Burnham told BBC London's political editor Karl Mercer that Sir Mark "certainly has a point and it needs to be heard".

"It's a matter for the courts when these decisions are made," the prime minister said. "They need to hear the voice of the commissioner of the Metropolitan Police.

"This case is disturbing and I would ask those working across the criminal justice system to look at it and make any necessary changes as a result."

Burnham also told BBC London the plan to release some offenders before the end of their custodial sentences, to free up space in prisons, was "not an ideal situation".

"The failure to build prison spaces over a number of years has led to this unacceptable situation," he said.

Dogan had pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images, which are the most serious.

He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.

According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window.

Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims.

"The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives.

"We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles."

News.title: White House bans CNN from Air Force One for Trump trip to Tennessee: report
News.content:

The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee, according to a new report.

Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network, along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.

In the latest roadblock, CNN was barred from Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday, two people familiar with the matter told The Washington Post.

CNN journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported.

open image in gallery The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.

But CNN was allowed coverage of Trump and Xi’s visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network’s coverage of Trump’s Knoxville trip.

Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them “fake news.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

open image in gallery Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network, along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events ( Getty Images )

The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges. But the outlets’ reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning.

A White House official later told the court that the press office started “reinstating” press badges that morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.

Bill Clinton, whose presidency was thrown into turmoil over an affair with a young staffer, has admitted there were times he wanted to ban the press from the White House, as President Donald Trump recently did, but he refrained.

“There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said to laughter at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week. “And there's a reason we have a constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

Clinton was likely referring to his affair with Monica Lewinsky, which rocked Washington in the late 1990s and — following allegations of a cover-up by the then-president — led to his impeachment in December 1998. He was later acquitted by the Senate.

The Democrat’s comments came after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because of unfavorable coverage.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social last Friday.

open image in gallery Bill Clinton, whose presidency was thrown into turmoil over an affair with a young staffer, has admitted there were times he wanted to ban the press from the White House, as President Donald Trump recently did, but he refrained ( AFP via Getty Images )

Lewinsky was a 22-year-old intern at the White House when she began an affair with Clinton, who was nearly 30 years her senior and married to Hillary Clinton.

Lewinsky recalled the moment the news of her clandestine relationship with the president broke during a February 2025 interview with Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper.

“I remember opening the door — and these were in the days where people would get a newspaper delivered and in D.C. it was always several like The [Washington] Post and The New York Times — I remember seeing my name above the fold…and looking down the hall and seeing the exact same newspaper outside everybody else's door,” Lewinsky said.

“It was shocking, it was terrifying and I didn't actually know how to process anything and really it was a moment where life as I knew it was over.”

open image in gallery The Democrat’s comments came after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because of unfavorable coverage ( Getty Images )

Trump has faced his own fair share of scandals that the media has covered, including two impeachments and multiple criminal indictments — one of which involved a hush money payment to a porn star.

His administration has also been criticized for its massive, hardline immigration crackdown and its war in Iran, which has caused gas prices to soar.

Unlike Clinton during the height of his sex scandal, when Trump faced scrutiny from the press, he decided to ban several outlets from covering his daily activities, calling them “fake news.”

open image in gallery 'There's a reason we have a constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off', Clinton said in an apparent jab at Trump ( Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative )

CNN, MS NOW and Politico subsequently filed a lawsuit to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.

But the outlets were still denied access at times, causing their journalists to reportedly miss Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state Dinner Thursday.

“The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López, who said she was not allowed to cover Xi’s arrival, told network host Symone Sanders Townsend.

Kimi Antonelli showed the first dent in his world championship armour after he crashed out of qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The Italian has reigned supreme so far this season, winning eight of the 14 rounds staged to secure an 81-point lead. But the 20-year-old committed his first major error in his title quest when he misjudged the opening corner and hit the wall in Baku.

Antonelli thudded the barrier on entry to the first turn, sustaining terminal damage to his Mercedes. He attempted to limp back to the pits but was instructed by race engineer Peter Bonnington to park his stricken machine.

His accident, which is set to leave him 16th on the grid, allows George Russell the chance to take pole position and chip into his team-mate’s title advantage.

TikTok will pay the state of Alabama at least $100 million and must implement a slew of safety features for teens in the state as part of a settlement agreement reached just before the case was set to go to trial.

Alabama sued the social media company in 2025 claiming that the platform had negative effects on the mental well-being of youths.

The lawsuit argued that TikTok's “addictive properties” — namely its algorithm that curates highly specific content catered to users' interests — were harmful to children and that the company knew of those harms.

Through the settlement, TikTok will make several platform-level changes for teen users in Alabama, including the option for teens to select a non-personalized content feed.

The platform will also bar cosmetic procedure filters for teens, implement a two-hour daily time limit and ban nighttime use from midnight to 6 a.m. Young users in Alabama will also be prompted to take a “productive pause” after 15 minutes of continuous use, and again at 60 and 90 minutes.

In addition to the platform changes, TikTok will pay Alabama $100 million in restitution and remediation, which will likely go toward funding youth mental health services and other programs. If enough other states reach qualifying settlements with TikTok within a specific time frame, Alabama could receive up to an additional $183.8 million.

The platform-level changes outlined in the settlement agreement are roughly similar to changes Meta agreed to make when it reached a settlement this summer to resolve similar claims that were filed by nearly every state, including Alabama. Meta had called on TikTok and its other chief competitor, YouTube, to join it in adopting similar standards, but TikTok had not publicly responded.

Katherine Robertson, chief counsel in the Alabama Attorney General’s office and the Republican nominee to be the state’s next attorney general, acknowledged the similarities with the Meta agreement and told The Associated Press on Friday: “There's been a war on childhood coming from a million different directions.”

“We recognize that parents and youth are fighting a battle against a bunch of different platforms,” Robertson said. “They’re manipulating kids to get addicted to their product, essentially.”

The settlement also outlines more robust and user-friendly parental controls, stronger age verification measures TikTok must take, and stronger content moderation protocols. Teen accounts will also be set to private by default.

A spokesperson for the TikTok USDS Joint Venture said Friday in a statement that TikTok’s priority has “always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community. This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens.”

Alabama would have been the first state to argue its claims against TikTok in front of a jury. The trial was scheduled to begin Monday.

TikTok has settled several lawsuits with similar claims filed by individuals before they went to trial, most notably in the landmark social media addiction trial in Los Angeles earlier this year. The jury in that case found that YouTube and Meta designed their platforms to hook young users without concern for their well-being.

TikTok also reached a $400 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice in August, ending a 2024 lawsuit alleging the company violated federal children’s privacy laws.

Associated Press writer Kim Chandler contributed to this report from Montgomery, Ala.

A prosecutor who has been accused of misconduct over a failed attempt to bring felony charges against six protesters of the federal immigration crackdown in Chicago has resigned, saying she was being treated as a scapegoat after the case fell apart.

In a scathing letter Thursday to Andrew Boutros, the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, prosecutor Sheri Mecklenburg wrote that she was “retiring under protest.”

“You have forced me to choose between remaining silent while my professional reputation is destroyed and prematurely surrendering my cherished career," Mecklenburg wrote in the letter obtained by The Associated Press. "I choose the latter.”

Mecklenburg accused Boutros of “laying responsibility at my feet for a felony prosecution that you personally directed over my objection that the case was better suited to misdemeanor charges.”

“I was a convenient target to be scapegoated and publicly vilified,” she wrote.

Boutros’ office did not immediately return a request for comment on the letter. Joel Bertocchi, an attorney for Mecklenburg, declined to comment.

During protests last fall against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the Chicago area, Boutros' office moved to press felony charges against six people for allegedly conspiring to impede an officer during a protest at an immigration detention facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

A grand jury twice refused to indict the group after Mecklenburg, an attorney on the case, presented them with evidence.

In the following months, the charges fell apart, and in May, Boutros dismissed the case altogether. It was among a string of cases in which the Trump administration leveled charges at anti-immigration enforcement protesters that did not ultimately stick.

The protesters, who have come to be known as the “Broadview Six,” have accused Mecklenburg of prosecutorial misconduct in her interactions with jury members, and have asked U.S. District Judge April M. Perry to consider sanctions on her. Perry is scheduled to hear oral arguments in the case Oct. 1.

In a motion filed Thursday, Mecklenburg informed the court of her retirement and asked to appear as an independent party in the case. The U.S. Attorney’s Office had previously barred her from filing “anything on her behalf” and told her she “could be disciplined or terminated if she did so," the motion read.

Terence Campbell, an attorney for Andre Martin, one of the former defendants, said Mecklenburg's “forced resignation letter raises a number of serious factual disputes" between her account and that of Boutros' office about why the case was brought.

___

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday signed an order banning fixed-odds betting just over a week ahead of the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.

The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting. The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until Oct. 5 to withdraw their funds.

Lula's government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offenses related to fixed-odds betting — the most common and dominant type of online sports betting — such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit bettors.

“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in Sao Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumor, or the tumor will kill us.”

Lula had also criticized the betting industry earlier this week at the United Nations General Assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes.”

Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread endorsement among Brazilians. Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula's main rival in the upcoming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure.”

Brazil's president has sharply criticized online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. Backlash grew during the FIFA World Cup when s were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.

Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8 billion reais ($7 billion) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.

The country's central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30 billion reais ($5.7 billion) on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare program Bolsa Familia (Family Grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.

Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.

Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro's father.

In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked over 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organizations like the First Command of the Capital from Sao Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.

Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to both close a drain to the country's economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.

Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4 billion per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.

Ahead of Friday’s move, Brazil's main soccer clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned clubs that sponsorships will end immediately if the government bans betting.

They said the move could mean “the end of Brazilian soccer," a claim mocked by some social media users in the soccer-mad country.
