World.title: Meeting in Mexico City, Sheinbaum and South Korea’s president pledge deeper ties
World.content:
Listen to this article

Visiting South Korean leader Lee Jae Myung and his Mexican counterpart, President Claudia Sheinbaum, agreed Thursday to deepen their bilateral relationship through a new roadmap focused on economic and financial cooperation, trade and technology.

In a joint press conference at Mexico City’s National Palace, the two presidents announced the signing of 17 agreements that included expanded cooperation in artificial intelligence, aerospace, energy, defense and supply chains.

Lee’s visit took place as Mexico seeks to diversify its economic relations amid international trade tensions and negotiations with the United States, its main partner, and as it promotes Sheinbaum’s Plan México to attract investment and increase national production.

During the press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that bilateral trade reached US $27 billion in 2025, pointing out that South Korea is one of Mexico’s top five trading partners worldwide, while Mexico is the Asian nation’s main partner in Latin America.

“The goal of greater complementary economic cooperation between our countries will generate shared prosperity and benefits for our people,” Sheinbaum said, adding that South Korean investment since 2006 topped US $11.5 billion.

Lee — the first South Korean leader to visit Mexico since 2010 — said both countries agreed to finalize the review of their reciprocal investment promotion and protection agreement, in order to strengthen economic ties.

“Mexico, the world’s 10th-largest economy and a hub of the global supply chain, is a highly important strategic partner for Korea,” Lee said.

The agreements signed range from economic and financial cooperation, to science and technology, as well as agriculture, security, intellectual property, culture, tourism and academic exchange.

Sheinbaum and Lee committed to promoting trade and investment and facilitating the integration of Mexican small and medium-sized enterprises into the supply chains of South Korean companies operating in Mexico.

Both governments also adopted a Mexico-Korea Action Plan 2026-2030 and will seek to complete the review of the agreement on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments “in the short term … in order to facilitate trade.”

Lee also announced talks to create a US $100 million credit scheme to facilitate Mexican companies’ acquisition of goods and services from Korean companies and to support South Korean firms operating in Mexico.

Yes, K-pop was on the agenda

At the same time, the two countries agreed to expand their cultural and educational exchanges, including the possibility of establishing a K-pop culture center in Mexico and a Mexican cultural institute in South Korea.

On that topic, Sheinbaum announced that K-pop superstars BTS will return to Mexico next year, adding that Stray Kids (a popular South Korean boy band) was to perform at Mexico City’s Estadio GNP Seguros on Friday.

Although BTS has not officially confirmed a return visit to Mexico, Sheinbaum said the group had accepted her proposal during their visit to the National Palace in May.

With reports from EFE, El Universal and Billboard

World.title: Tabasco homicides dropped over 50% since 2024, officials report: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Sheinbaum on tour: As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco.

As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco. 📉 Homicides down 54% in Tabasco : National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day.

: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day. 🚔 Over 6,500 arrests since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period. 🔻 La Barredora “greatly diminished” : Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.”

: Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.” 🗨️ Sheinbaum weighs in on Trump-Xi meeting: The president called Thursday’s meeting in Washington between Trump and Xi “very interesting.” She warned that rivalry between the two powers creates global uncertainty and reaffirmed Mexico’s preference for “peace and cooperation for development.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Villahermosa, capital of the Gulf Coast state of Tabasco.

Security officials presented data showing that the federal government has made significant progress in combating violence in the state, including through the arrest of alleged criminals accused of fueling it. Officials reasserted that the government’s security strategy is yielding results in Tabasco and across the country.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments on the meeting in Washington, D.C., on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum will join both leaders, and various others, at the APEC Summit in China in November.

Government reports 54% reduction in homicides compared to 2024 peak

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that the daily homicide rate in Tabasco in August was 1.6, a reduction of 54% compared to November 2024, the month with the highest murder rate —3.5 per day — since the current federal government took office in October 2024.

“Thanks to the strengthening of the national public security strategy and coordination with the state government, a reduction in this crime has been achieved,” she said.

According to the data Figueroa presented, the year-over-year decline in homicides in August was 16%.

Figueroa also reported that Tabasco has recorded an average of 10.3 high-impact crimes per day so far in 2026.

That figure represents a decline of 12% compared to 2025 and a reduction of 18% compared to 2024. Among the offenses classified as high-impact crimes are homicides, kidnappings, acts of extortion, violent robberies and rape.

More than 6,000 people arrested in Tabasco since October 2024

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that more than 6,500 people — 6,527 to be exact — were arrested in Tabasco between Oct. 1, 2024 and Sept. 15, 2026.

Data he presented showed that 2,053 firearms and 12.97 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period.

García Harfuch said that the arrest of “important targets” in Tabasco has had a “direct impact on the reduction of violence.”

He mentioned a number of the most significant arrests that have been made in the state, including that of a man accused of nine homicides.

García Harfuch: La Barredora has been weakened

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the current strength in Tabasco of La Barredora, a criminal group that was formerly allegedly led by ex-Tabasco Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena.

Bermúdez, who served as security minister in the state government led by former Governor Adán Augusto López Hernández, was arrested in Paraguay in September 2024 and subsequently extradited to Mexico, where he is in prison awaiting trial. López, a Morena party senator and former federal interior minister, has faced claims from opposition parties that he was also involved in La Barredora when the group was allegedly led by Bermúdez.

García Harfuch said there have been “a lot of arrests” of people linked to the criminal group. He subsequently praised the Tabasco state police for their efforts to combat organized crime.

“This organization is greatly diminished,” he said, referring to La Barredora.

“It’s practically split in two,” García Harfuch said.

Sheinbaum comments on Trump-Xi meeting

A reporter asked the president about the meeting on Thursday between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, noting that the latter stated that China and the United States must maintain a peaceful relationship and engage in “healthy” competition.

Sheinbaum described the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents as “very interesting.”

“… The idea of rivalry between two important nations such as China and the United States creates uncertainty in the world,” she said.

“And what Mexico has always sought is peace and cooperation for development,” Sheinbaum added.

She said that her government’s view is that economic competition shouldn’t create “rivalries between countries.”

Mexico has important economic relationships with both the United States and China. Mexico and the United States are each other’s largest trading partner, while China is a large exporter of goods to Mexico.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Cano’s ‘Malinche’: A musical that’s not all song and dance
World.content:
Just about every evening for the past year and a half, more than 1,000 people have made their way to El Frontón, a century-old Art Deco theatre in Mexico City’s small but historic enclave, Tabacalera.

There, the musical, “Malinche,” has been in full swing, having recently kicked off its second run on Aug. 15, with more than 80 cast members singing and dancing flamenco, urban, hip-hop and contemporary to the vision of Jesús Carmona, donning face paint, leather crop tops and fringed two-pieces in an auditorium seating 1,299.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MALINCHE EL MUSICAL (@malinchethemusical)

Created, written and directed by Nacho Cano, the show entered the Mexican theatre scene in March 2025 after a two-and-a-half-year run in Madrid, where it was housed in the IFEMA complex.

It wasn’t exactly Cano’s vision, who unsuccessfully pitched for a 30-meter Aztec-inspired pyramid in Hortaleza, but the venue was still kitted out with a small pyramid, cenotes, pyrotechnics and live bands, making a sizeable impression in Spain’s commercial theatre market.

Since its opening night, though, “Malinche” has faced backlash for what some consider historically insensitive depictions of the 1519 Spanish Conquest, including its retelling of Aztec emperor Moctezuma’s Christian awakening.

The controversy surrounding “Malinche” requires a discussion that centers not only its account of the titular Nahua woman, but also the political background of those who paved the way for its success.

Navigating the history and identity of Malinche

Much of popular art cannot be separated from its contemporary political milieu, both socially and geographically, and Nacho Cano’s work is no exception.

It was just seven years ago that then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador sought an apology from Spain’s King Felipe VI over the colonial treatment of Indigenous Mexicans. After he failed to deliver such an apology, the king was subsequently excluded from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s inauguration, though he has since acknowledged that “there were significant abuses.”

Often described to those who don’t know her as the “Mexican Pocahontas,” it is widely understood that Malintzin, Doña Marina (her Christian name), or Malinche was an Indigenous woman who became Hernán Cortés’ interpreter and thus played a critical role during Spain’s conquest. Around 14 years old when she met Cortés, Malinche would eventually give birth to their son.

In no uncertain terms, Malinche’s history has been written for her. There is no surviving account from her own voice, only skewed and holey Spanish and Nahuatl accounts of the conquest. As an interpreter pushed into slavery, a potential informant of the Cholula massacre, or a willful lover — depending on who you ask — Malinche’s story becomes warped and warbled on the tongues of many.

A contested icon across modern political agendas

Like any cultural paradigm, scholars have attempted to categorize her perception and presentation both temporally and by groups supporting varying ideologies.

A traditional nationalist slant views Malinche as a traitor, “La Chingada,” taking on an Eve-like persona in her betrayal of the nation for the conquistadors, ultimately facilitating the tragic end of the Mexica. Others stress her victimhood not only at the hands of her oppressors but also in her literary portrayal as a traitor.

Here we see, through the abstraction of Malinche, the reduction of the female to a single narrative. Her portrayal even inspired the neologism “malinchista,” which refers to those favoring foreign cultures and ideals.

Meanwhile, feminist and Chicanx discourse have outlined Malinche’s dynamic representation in alignment with varying political agendas and strived to empower her agency. Many view her as a victim of colonial patriarchy who, as scholar Gloria Anzaldúa described it, exists beyond the “traditional/treacherous binary,” and chose to “be a survivor” who “cast her lot with the Spaniards to ensure survival of a race.”

Other postcolonial scholars take on such subaltern perspectives but question Malinche’s true autonomy, often highlighting the backdrop of religious colonial values of benevolence that Malinche was constructed and demonized against.

Acutely relevant, a pro-Hispanic and contemporary transformation of the narrative sees Malinche much like Disney portrays Pocahontas — a young woman whose love for the heroic Western explorer enabled the birth of the mestizaje, making her the “mother” of Mexico.

And so enters Nacho Cano, creator of “Malinche.”

Nacho Cano’s path from pop star to controversy

Ignacio “Nacho” Cano is a former member of the popular band Mecano, a luminary of Spain’s ’80s music scene and one of the biggest Spanish pop stars of the time. The band’s debut album sold 1 million copies in Spain alone, and they have since sold more than 30 million records worldwide.

Cano went on to develop the wildly influential “Hoy No Me Puedo Levantar,” a musical exploring Madrid’s post-Franco countercultural movement, La Movida, and one of the most financially successful Spanish musicals to date.

Despite his status as a 20th-century pop idol, Cano also established himself as a controversial political figure. He’s an avowed ally of the right-wing president of the Community of Madrid and People’s Party, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who presented him in 2021 with the Order of the Second of May.

Ayuso herself was described by Politico as being in a “nationalistic showdown with Mexico.”

Such political dissension stems from her admiration of Cortés and defense of the Spanish Conquest as a civilizing mission, perhaps most notably at this year’s “Celebration of Evangelization and Mestizaje in Mexico.”

Sheinbaum has rebuked Ayuso’s characterization of the “conquest as salvation,” while Ayuso has been dubbed by Morena party members “the heir to the Spanish Falange,” a far-right fascist political movement founded in Spain in the 1930s.

Cano has similarly argued that “without Cortés there would be no Mexico,” a sentiment reflected in the feathers and flashlights of his extravagant musical production.

Divided perspectives and powerful corporate backing

In July 2024, Cano was arrested for alleged improprieties and poor working conditions for the performers in Madrid’s “Malinche,” including undocumented immigrants. The charges were dropped the following year, with Cano insisting that left-wing leaders led an alleged coordinated attack.

Beyond the show itself, Cano offers viewers a more detailed insight into the 10-year process behind his play in the 2021 Netflix documentary, “Making Malinche,” a name whose very essence speaks volumes. Malinche is once again a woman methodically remade and reduced, this time to an unwavering, consensual lover.

In an interview with El Mundo, Cano argued that Mexico’s history has been told “deliberately poorly,” and claimed in the documentary that his work is more historically accurate.

The overarching narrative he perpetuates is that Malinche was not a betrayer, but a woman whose passionate love for a Spaniard gifted humanity the New World.

We have seen a correlation between Malinche’s shifting portrayal and shifting Mexican cultural identity, as critics argue Cano has both sanitized and romanticized the violent reality of Spanish conquest.

Left-wing critics have argued the musical erases Indigenous trauma and experience in its “perpetuat[ion] of a Eurocentric narrative,” describing it as a “spectacle of postmodern Falangism.”

On the other end of the spectrum, conservative critics have chided Cano for doing a disservice to Catholicism, accusing him of not pushing far enough “an authentic ode to the history of Spain, against ideological revisionism and the Black Legend,” a reference to a school of thought that suggests “anti-Catholic” and “anti-Spanish” narratives deliberately position the Spanish Empire as singularly motivated by cruelty and greed.

However, these are not the only reasons many people in the left-wing community have boycotted “Malinche.”

The champions of ‘Malinche’

Ricardo Salinas Pliego, a Mexican television magnate and chairman of Grupo Salinas whose net worth is estimated to be US $5 billion, is responsible for bringing “Malinche” to Mexico and promoting it on his network, TV Azteca. His wife, María Laura Medina de Salinas, served as an executive producer during its opening in Mexico last year, after falling “in love” with it in Madrid and “form[ing] a synergy” with Cano, according to José Manuel Azpiroz, the director of communications at Salinas’ Grupo Elektra.

What’s more, the show is officially “presented” by Banco Azteca, part of Salinas’ conglomerate.

Much like Cano, Salinas is no stranger to controversy, having been accused of tax evasion to the tune of US $3 billion while also flirting with a presidential run.

Once labeled “the newest face of the Mexican new right,” he is an outspoken critic of Sheinbaum and supporter of the National Action Party (PAN), with a political temperament that follows in the footsteps of Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Salinas and Cano also have close ties to Juan Miguel Zunzunegui, a Mexican historian and avid rejector of the Black Legend. He defends the Spanish empire and upholds a history that dismisses Indigenous suffering and denies the mass violation of women.

In an interview with El Mundo, he said, “[t]he Spaniard who thinks they did horrible things in America does so out of ignorance.”

Cano recently wrote the prologue to Zunzunegui’s book, “Hernán Cortés,” and Zunzunegui is involved in the current run of “Malinche,” making a special appearance as Spanish friar and translator Jerónimo de Aguilar.

Turning historical violence into a love story

Malinche’s representation has been utilized as a vehicle to express specific sociopolitical ideologies within Mexican society, both at home and abroad. The question now is why proponents of “Malinche” feel a desire to promote a history of colonial violence as a love story that’s couched in consent and results in creation?

Some have asked a similar question of Disney’s romanticization of colonial relationships in its 1995 adaptation of “Pocahontas,” with the understanding that depicting a “mutually satisfying encounter” legitimizes what they describe as the violence of Western history.

“Malinche” too warrants consideration as part of a broader ideological posture seeking to sublimate Spain’s imperial legacy. However, with its second season running through January 2027, its popularity, devoid of nuanced conversations about who gets to write and rewrite history, speaks for itself.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS 2026, 25 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —The country — Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and most populous country, with about 210 million people. It elects a president on Sunday 4 October, with a runoff three weeks later when nobody wins outright. —The background — President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva seeks a fourth term. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro carries the conservative banner after his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, was barred from running and imprisoned. —Why it is news — Nine days before the vote, the country’s most traditional pollster confirms a stable first-round picture while its runoff reading is a two-point statistical tie. Five other institutes released the same week disagree with each other by more than any margin of error. —What happened — Datafolha published its latest national wave on Thursday 24 September 2026: Lula 40 percent, Flávio Bolsonaro 36 percent in the first round, and 47 to 45 for Lula in a runoff. —The numbers — Datafolha heard 2,002 voters in person between 22 and 24 September, with a margin of error of two points. The survey is registered with the Superior Electoral Court as BR-00304/2026. —What it means for you — Read the race as a band, not a number. If you hold Brazilian assets or plan to relocate, prepare for either man to win rather than for the leader of the latest survey.

Sources: Datafolha national poll released 24 September 2026 (TSE registration BR-00304/2026, fieldwork 22–24 September, 2,002 in-person interviews, ±2pp); AtlasIntel/Bloomberg (fieldwork 17–22 September); Palver (20–23 September); PoderData/Aya (20–23 September); Futura/100% Cidades (19–23 September); Alfa Inteligência (18–23 September); Rio Times poll tracker, 25 September 2026.

The spontaneous reading, where voters name a candidate without being shown a list, tells the same story in rougher form. Lula leads 36 percent to 27 percent, and 4 percent still name the imprisoned Jair Bolsonaro, who is not on the ballot. Those votes are the pool Flávio Bolsonaro still hopes to consolidate before 4 October.

A Two-Point Runoff Is a Coin Toss

Datafolha’s runoff simulation has Lula ahead 47 percent to 45 percent. With a margin of error of two points on each number, that is a statistical tie: the true gap could be four points for Lula or one point for Flávio Bolsonaro. Treat it as a coin toss, not a forecast.

The other institutes released this week frame the band. AtlasIntel/Bloomberg has the runoff at Lula 47.7, Flávio 47.4. Alfa Inteligência records an exact 43–43 tie. At the other end, Palver puts Flávio ahead 48–45 and Futura/100% Cidades shows his widest lead at 49.4–43.7. The houses disagree with each other by far more than any single margin of error, which is why our Brazil election polls tracker reads them as a range rather than an average.

The Understudies Fare No Better

Datafolha also tested the runners-up as if they were the conservative standard-bearer. Lula would tie Ronaldo Caiado at 46–44 and Flávio Cury at 46–43, and he would beat both Romeu Zema and Renan Santos by identical 48–39 margins. Swapping the challenger, in other words, does not change the shape of the race.

That matters for the Liberal Party’s internal argument. Flávio Bolsonaro’s numbers are not visibly weaker than any tested alternative, which strengthens his claim to stay in through 4 October even if the first round goes against him.

What Comes Next

The next major reading lands on Saturday 26 September, when Veritá releases its national survey with 40,500 interviews — by far the largest sample of this campaign and the one with the finest regional cuts. Our tracker will carry it the moment it drops.

Brazil votes in the first round on Sunday 4 October 2026, choosing a president, 54 of 81 senators and all 513 federal deputies. If no candidate takes more than half the valid votes, the top two meet again on Sunday 25 October.

World.title: Best Time to Visit Brazil 2026: Weather and Seasons by Region
World.content:
BRAZIL · TRAVEL & EXPATS

Key Facts —Short answer For Rio and the Southeast, April to June and September to November. For the Pantanal, May to October. For the Amazon, July to December. There is no single best month for the whole country. —Peak season December to March: hot, humid, crowded and the most expensive weeks of the year, especially around Carnival and New Year. —Carnival 2027 Runs February 5 to 10 in Rio; the top samba schools parade February 7 to 9, the champions on February 13. —Cheapest window May, June, September and October usually bring lower hotel rates, outside the July school holidays. —Entry rules Citizens of the US, Canada and Australia need an e-visa (US$80.90, online) since April 10, 2025. Most EU and UK passports do not. —Demand Brazil welcomed a record 9.3 million international visitors in 2025, and 5.26 million in the first half of 2026, so book peak dates early.

The best time to visit Brazil depends on the region, not the country: for Rio de Janeiro and the Southeast, go in the shoulder months of April to June or September to November, when the weather is warm but mild and crowds thin out. If your trip is about wildlife in the Pantanal, choose the dry season from May to October, and for the Amazon, July to December.

Copacabana beach in Rio de Janeiro. For Rio and the Southeast, the best travel windows are April to June and September to November.

That is the honest version of a question most travel sites answer with a single month. Brazil is roughly the size of Western Europe, spans five climate zones, and its seasons are inverted from the northern hemisphere: summer runs from December to February, winter from June to August.

What follows is a region-by-region breakdown for late 2026 and 2027, with the event dates, price patterns and entry rules that actually change your planning. All figures are as of September 2026.

The quick answer, region by region

Region Best window Why Rio & Southeast Apr–Jun, Sep–Nov Mild 24–29°C days, less rain, lower rates than summer Northeast (Bahia, Recife, Fortaleza) Sep–Mar Driest, breeziest stretch; warm year-round Pantanal May–Oct (peak Jul–Sep) Dry season concentrates wildlife; best jaguar sightings Amazon Jul–Dec Lower water opens trails and river beaches Iguaçu Falls May–Sep Most comfortable; fullest flow after summer rains South (Florianópolis, Gramado) Oct–Apr for beaches Real winters Jun–Aug; wine country charm then

Rio de Janeiro and the Southeast

Rio is a year-round city, but it has two clearly better windows. From April to June and again from September to November, daytime temperatures sit around 24–29°C, the humidity eases, and you share Ipanema with residents rather than the entire southern cone.

Summer, from December to March, is the postcard version – highs of 30–35°C and packed beaches – but it is also Rio’s rainiest stretch. Short, violent afternoon downpours are routine, and hotel rates peak, especially between Christmas and Carnival.

Winter (June to August) is mild, not cold: expect 18–25°C in Rio, cooler evenings, and the odd cloudy spell. It is a genuinely good time for the city if you do not need a tan, and rates drop outside the July school holidays.

The Northeast: the all-year beach answer

Salvador, Recife, Fortaleza and the beach towns of Bahia and Ceará stay warm all year, typically 26–32°C. The driest and brightest months run roughly from September to March; June and July bring the region’s main rainy spell, usually as short showers rather than washouts.

If your Brazil trip is fundamentally a beach trip, the Northeast is the region that lets you ignore the calendar – and the one most foreign visitors under-book.

The Pantanal: May to October, no debate

The world’s largest tropical wetland floods between roughly November and April – more than 70% of its rain falls from December to March – which scatters the wildlife and closes stretches of the access roads.

In the dry season from May to October, and especially July to September, animals concentrate around shrinking water sources. That is when jaguars, giant otters, capybaras and hyacinth macaws become reliably visible. Days are hot, around 30–35°C, but June and July mornings can drop close to 5–10°C – pack a jacket for dawn safaris.

The Amazon: pick your water level

It rains in the Amazon in every month – it is a rainforest. The practical choice is between low water (roughly July to December in the Manaus region), when trails open, river beaches appear and hiking is easier, and high water (January to June), when the rivers rise by 10 metres or more and boats can glide through flooded forest you cannot reach any other way.

First-time visitors usually prefer the drier months of July to October. Photographers and boat-focused travelers often prefer the flooded season. Neither is wrong.

Iguaçu Falls and the South

The falls run fullest after the summer rains from December to March, but that is also when heat, humidity and crowds peak. May to September trades a little water volume for far more comfortable visiting conditions – and the falls remain enormous. Avoid Easter week and July if you dislike queues.

Further south, Florianópolis works as a beach destination from October to April. The mountain towns of Rio Grande do Sul and the wine country have real four-season weather, with occasional winter frost – charming in June and July, but pack accordingly.

If you are traveling for an event

Some trips are built around dates, not weather. The fixed points through 2027:

Réveillon (New Year’s Eve): December 31, with over a million people on Copacabana beach. Book months ahead.

December 31, with over a million people on Copacabana beach. Book months ahead. Carnival 2027: February 5 to 10. In Rio, the top-tier samba schools parade at the Sambadrome on February 7, 8 and 9; the champions’ parade follows on February 13. Grandstand tickets start around US$38, but accommodation is the real constraint – Rio hotels sell out and apply minimum stays, often at double or triple normal rates.

February 5 to 10. In Rio, the top-tier samba schools parade at the Sambadrome on February 7, 8 and 9; the champions’ parade follows on February 13. Grandstand tickets start around US$38, but accommodation is the real constraint – Rio hotels sell out and apply minimum stays, often at double or triple normal rates. Rock in Rio: the festival’s September editions turn the city into a two-weekend event; the 2026 edition ran September 4 to 13, and the next is expected in 2028.

the festival’s September editions turn the city into a two-weekend event; the 2026 edition ran September 4 to 13, and the next is expected in 2028. FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027: Brazil hosts the tournament from June 24 to July 25, 2027, with matches in Rio, São Paulo and six other cities – expect June–July 2027 demand and prices to behave like a second high season.

When it is cheapest

Outside Carnival, New Year and the July school holidays, Brazil’s low season runs roughly May to September. The sweet spots for value are May, June, September and October: decent weather in most regions, visibly lower hotel rates, and far easier bookings.

One structural note: distances in Brazil are continental. Rio to Manaus is a four-hour flight, and domestic fares spike around Brazilian holidays. A multi-region itinerary costs less in the shoulder months partly because of those fares.

The paperwork, before the weather

Since April 10, 2025, citizens of the United States, Canada and Australia need an electronic visitor visa to enter Brazil – applied for online at the official portal (brazil.vfsevisa.com) for US$80.90. US e-visas are valid for ten years, Canadian and Australian ones for five, with stays of up to 90 days per visit. Most EU, UK, New Zealand and South American passports remain visa-exempt. Apply before booking non-refundable travel: airlines will not board you without an approved e-visa.

If you are weighing a longer stay rather than a visit, see our guides to moving to Brazil in 2026 and the cost of living in Brazil by city.

The honest downsides

No month is perfect everywhere, and some trade-offs are real:

Summer means rain. December to March is beach weather between downpours, not instead of them. Rio’s summer storms can flood streets within an hour.

December to March is beach weather between downpours, not instead of them. Rio’s summer storms can flood streets within an hour. Peak pricing is extreme. Carnival and New Year hotel rates in Rio routinely double or triple, with minimum stays of four nights or more.

Carnival and New Year hotel rates in Rio routinely double or triple, with minimum stays of four nights or more. July is a hidden high season. Brazilian school holidays fill the Pantanal, Iguaçu and the winter resorts, even though foreign arrivals dip.

Brazilian school holidays fill the Pantanal, Iguaçu and the winter resorts, even though foreign arrivals dip. The South gets genuinely cold. June to August in Rio Grande do Sul means single-digit temperatures at times, not a mild Mediterranean winter.

June to August in Rio Grande do Sul means single-digit temperatures at times, not a mild Mediterranean winter. Distances punish improvisation. You cannot “add the Amazon” to a Rio weekend. Multi-region trips need flight legs booked in advance, and fares climb around holidays.

You cannot “add the Amazon” to a Rio weekend. Multi-region trips need flight legs booked in advance, and fares climb around holidays. 2027 will be busier than 2026. Brazil is coming off a record 9.3 million international visitors in 2025 (+37% year on year) and 5.26 million in the first half of 2026, per Embratur – and the Women’s World Cup lands in June 2027. Book headline dates early.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best month to visit Brazil?

There is no single best month for the whole country. For Rio and the Southeast, May, September and October balance weather, prices and crowds. For the Pantanal, August and September are prime wildlife months.

When is Carnival in Brazil in 2027?

Carnival 2027 runs from February 5 to 10. In Rio, the Grupo Especial samba schools parade at the Sambadrome on February 7, 8 and 9, and the champions’ parade is on February 13.

What is the cheapest time to visit Brazil?

May, June, September and October usually combine the lowest hotel and domestic flight prices with decent weather. Avoid Carnival, New Year and the July school holidays if budget matters.

Do I need a visa to visit Brazil in 2026?

US, Canadian and Australian citizens need an e-visa (US$80.90, online at brazil.vfsevisa.com) since April 10, 2025. Most EU, UK and South American nationalities remain visa-exempt for up to 90 days.

When is the best time to see jaguars in the Pantanal?

The dry season from May to October, with July to September the peak. Receding water concentrates wildlife around rivers and waterholes, which is when sightings become reliable.

Is Brazil worth visiting in winter (June to August)?

Yes, especially for the Pantanal, the Amazon, Iguaçu and the Northeast, where winter is dry and warm. Rio stays mild at 18–25°C. Only the far south gets properly cold.

How far in advance should I book Carnival 2027?

Four to six months for accommodation in Rio’s South Zone – by October 2026 at the latest. Sambadrome grandstand tickets start around US$38, but hotels are the bottleneck.

Sources: Visit Brasil/Embratur – international arrivals, first half of 2026 (Ministry of Tourism and Federal Police data, August 2026) · Brazilian Consulate-General in Miami (gov.br) – e-visa rules and US$80.90 fee, in force since April 10, 2025 · Rio The Guide – Carnival 2027 dates per LIESA parade calendar · Lonely Planet – Brazil seasonal guide, March 2026 · The Rio Times – Rio Carnival guide, Rock in Rio 2026 guide, Brazil coverage. Prices and dates as of September 2026; weather patterns are historical norms, and actual conditions vary year to year.

World.title: Brazil Launches Plan to Buy Old Household Debts at 90% Off Before Vote
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

BRAZIL · HOUSEHOLD DEBT

Key Facts — The country Brazil has more than 210 million people and Latin America’s largest economy, roughly the size of Italy’s. About 84 million Brazilians have at least one overdue debt on record.

— Why it matters Household loan defaults reached 5.8% in July, the highest since the central bank’s series began in 2011. Repayments swallow a record 28.9% of family income.

— Why now Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October. President Lula da Silva, seeking a fourth term, is running close to Flávio Bolsonaro. Polls cite household debt as a drag on his approval.

— What happened On Friday 25 September in São Paulo, the government launched Desenrola 3.0. The state will buy old household debts from banks at auction, expecting discounts of at least 90%.

— The numbers The target is R$150 billion (about US$29 billion) of debt, half of an eligible R$300 billion (about US$58 billion). The expected cost is R$15 billion (about US$2.9 billion).

— What it means for you There is nothing to 

— Still open The measure’s text and number, income limits, repayment terms, how many people benefit, and whether election law allows it before the vote.

Brazil’s government on Friday launched Desenrola 3.0, a plan to buy old household debts that banks no longer expect to recover. It was announced in São Paulo on 25 September, alongside a ban on online betting.

The state aims to buy R$150 billion (about US$29 billion) of overdue loans for about R$15 billion (about US$2.9 billion). The launch came nine days before a presidential first round in which Lula is running close to his main rival.

Christmas shoppers crowd Rua 25 de Março, a discount shopping street in central São Paulo, in an earlier year. (Photo: Marcelo Camargo/Agência Brasil)

What the government announced

At the event, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a provisional measure banning online betting. Finance Minister Dario Durigan then announced the new debt programme.

A provisional measure is a decree with the force of law that lapses unless Congress approves it within 120 days. The daily Estadão reported that Desenrola 3.0 was also launched by provisional measure.

Its number and text had not appeared in the Diário Oficial, the official gazette, by 7:30 pm Brasília time. Planning and Budget Minister Bruno Moretti presented the details, according to the news site Brasil 247.

Moretti said the November auction depends on the signing of the provisional measure presented to the president, Brasil 247 reported. No outlet had yet confirmed that it was signed.

Lula said the new round was better than the last two. “Now it is the government that will buy the debt and sort out people’s lives,” he said, as quoted by Estadão.

Desenrola, roughly “untangle,” is the brand of Lula’s debt-relief rounds since 2023. On 17 September Durigan had told the newspaper Extra that this plan should not carry the name, because Desenrola meant renegotiation.

How the debt purchase works

Banks will be invited to sell bundles of unpaid loans to the state at auction. “The one that sells its portfolio at the biggest discount wins,” Moretti said, according to Brasil 247.

The buyer will be the National Treasury or a federal bank such as Banco do Brasil or Caixa. The first auction is planned for November, O Globo and Brasil 247 reported.

Moretti said such portfolios already trade at discounts of about 90% to 95%, because banks struggle to collect them. He put that market at about R$50 billion (about US$9.7 billion) a year.

The discount will be passed on to debtors. “These discounts will be passed directly to the families,” Moretti said.

This is not a write-off, InfoMoney and O Globo reported. Once the state buys a debt, the credit record is lifted, but the debtor owes the Treasury a reduced sum.

Repayments would carry lower interest in instalments matched to income, according to InfoMoney. Moretti gave no income limits, instalment terms or interest rates, Brasil 247 noted.

In Brazil, a debtor in default is listed by credit bureaus such as Serasa and often cannot get new credit. Clearing that record is the plan’s main promise.

Which debts qualify

Eligible old household debts are credit-card balances, both revolving and instalment, and personal loans not deducted from payroll. They must be between two and four and a half years overdue.

Moretti also cited a two-to-four-year range in his summary, Brasil 247 noted. The upper limit therefore needs confirming in the legal text.

Moretti described them as, for example, debts of up to R$10,000 (about US$1,930), O Globo and Brasil 247 reported. Whether that is a formal cap per debt awaits the legal text.

The age window matters. Under Brazil’s consumer code, a negative entry must be removed from credit-bureau records after five years.

The announced categories are bank debts. Unpaid water and power bills, which the first Desenrola covered, were not mentioned.

Before the launch, Folha de S.Paulo had reported a focus on debts of up to R$15,000 (about US$2,900) from 2020 to 2022. The Novo Desenrola, the second round, was limited to people earning up to five times the minimum wage.

What it will cost

The government puts the stock of such unpaid debt at R$300 billion (about US$58 billion). It aims to buy about half, or R$150 billion (about US$29 billion).

At a 90% discount, that costs the state about R$15 billion (about US$2.9 billion). At 95%, the top of today’s market, the bill would halve.

The official estimate is above the R$5 billion to R$10 billion (about US$970 million to US$1.9 billion) reported before the launch. No official explanation of the funding had been published by Friday evening.

Fabio Graner, a columnist at O Globo, wrote before the launch that such a purchase counts as primary spending. Brazil’s fiscal target is set on the primary balance, which excludes interest payments.

Valor Econômico, a business daily, had reported that the economic team intended to fit the cost inside the budget and fiscal rules.

How deep Brazil’s household debt runs

Serasa counted 83.98 million Brazilians in default in August, up just 0.06% from July. That equals about two in five Brazilians, children included.

Their overdue debts totalled R$586.4 billion (about US$113 billion) in July, according to Serasa. The R$150 billion (about US$29 billion) target is roughly a quarter of that.

Household loan defaults, meaning payments more than 90 days late, reached 5.8% in July. That was the highest since the series began in March 2011 (see Brazil’s Household Loan Delinquency Climbs to a July Record).

Repayments took a record 28.9% of family income in June. Total household debt that month stood at 49.8% of a year’s income, a tenth of a point below the record.

Earlier relief rounds helped but did not reverse the trend. The first Desenrola renegotiated about R$53 billion (about US$10 billion) for around 15 million people from 2023.

The Novo Desenrola renegotiated R$28.37 billion (about US$5.5 billion) from May and closed less than a month before the new launch. O Globo found 30.34% of its instalment deals behind on payments in September, a figure the ministry is checking.

The betting ban and credit rules

The same event ended legal online betting, as reported in Brazil Bans Online Betting: Deposits Stop, Sites Go Dark on 6 October. Deposits stop once the measure is published, and sites go offline on 6 October.

Durigan said more than R$60 billion (about US$11.6 billion) had gone to licensed betting firms. The government links that drain to household arrears.

Moretti said the debt measure also asks regulators, chiefly the central bank, to curb abusive lending, according to Brasil 247. Folha had reported that officials saw such safeguards as essential to stop relapse.

Central bank governor Gabriel Galípolo said this week that the bank was worried by “aggressive and predatory” credit offers.

The election and the critics

Brazil holds the first round of its presidential election on Sunday 4 October. Lula faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the right-wing Liberal Party, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Polls show a tight race, as in Brazil Poll Shows Lula Edging Flávio Bolsonaro 46% to 45% in a Runoff. A Datafolha poll on 24 September put Lula at 40% and Flávio at 36% in the first round.

O Globo counted six vote-friendly announcements this month, one every four days. They include a 15% rise in Bolsa Família cash transfers and larger fuel subsidies.

Flávio has promised a rival debt plan, SOS Brasil, with discounts of up to 90% through the state lender Caixa. He called the betting ban “hypocritical, electioneering and populist,” the news site Metrópoles reported.

No response from his campaign to Desenrola 3.0 itself had been reported by early evening.

Brazil’s Elections Law bans handing out free goods, money or benefits in an election year. The main exception is social programmes set in law and already funded the year before.

Government lawyers reviewed the design before the launch, Valor reported. It said the legal risk was greatest if debts were cancelled outright; the announced plan instead has families repay a reduced sum.

An O Globo editorial in May called the Desenrola relaunch “electioneering” and said repeated relief “punishes the good payer.” Durigan blames a “pandemic of debt” inherited from the previous government.

What comes next

The next step is the legal text in the Diário Oficial. It should confirm the rules, the debt-age limit and any cap per debt.

The Treasury or a federal bank must then run the November auction, after the 4 October first round. Debts would be restructured only after the purchase, Moretti said.

The plan does not make old household debts vanish. Debtors would still owe a reduced sum, and there is no sign-up yet.

Nor does it mean cheaper credit for everyone. It targets old debts that banks have given up on, not the repayments squeezing families who still pay on time.

The details to watch are the legal text, the auction rules, the income limits and the repayment terms. All conversions here use BRL 5.175 per US dollar (open.er-api.com, 25 September 2026).

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s Desenrola 3.0?

It is a plan, launched on 25 September 2026, for the state to buy old household debts from banks at auction. Debtors’ credit records are lifted, and they owe the Treasury a reduced sum.

Which debts qualify?

Credit-card debts, revolving and instalment, and personal loans not deducted from payroll, between two and four and a half years overdue. Income limits and any cap per debt await the legal text.

When will debts be bought?

The government plans the first auction for November 2026, run by the Treasury or a federal bank. There is no sign-up for debtors yet.

How much will it cost?

About R$15 billion (about US$2.9 billion), to buy R$150 billion (about US$29 billion) of debt at a 90% discount. The final cost depends on the discounts banks offer at auction.

Sources: O Globo (25 September 2026, reports by Tháis Barcellos and João Sorima, columns by Fabio Graner and a Míriam Leitão blog post); Extra and Reuters via Terra (25 September); Estadão/Broadcast (25 September); Valor Econômico (24 and 25 September); InfoMoney (25 September); CNN Brasil (25 September); Brasil 247 account of Bruno Moretti’s presentation (25 September); Metrópoles and g1 (25 September); Folha de S.Paulo (18 and 25 September); Extra interview with Dario Durigan (17 September); Serasa Mapa da Inadimplência (July and August 2026); Banco Central do Brasil credit statistics released 28 August 2026; Law 9.504/1997, article 73.

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

BRAZIL · ONLINE BETTING

Key Facts — The country Brazil has about 213 million people and an economy roughly the size of Canada’s. Within a year of licensing, it became one of the world’s largest online betting markets.

— Why it matters Sports betting was legalised in 2018 but only licensed from January 2025. Last year licensed sites kept R$37 billion (about US$7.1 billion) after paying prizes — in effect, what bettors lost.

— Why now The presidential election’s first round is on Sunday 4 October. Debt payments took a record 28.9 percent of household income in June, and Lula blames betting for much of it.

— What happened On Friday 25 September the government announced a ban on online betting and casino games by provisional measure, signed by Lula in São Paulo.

— The numbers Some 85 licensed companies, 25.2 million bettors in 2025 and R$9.95 billion (about US$1.9 billion) in federal taxes. Each company paid R$30 million (about US$5.8 million) for its licence.

— What it means for you No new deposits once the measure is published. Withdraw balances by 23:59 on 5 October; sites go dark on 6 October.

— Still open The gazette text, lawsuits by operators, licence-fee refunds, and whether Congress keeps the ban within 120 days.

Brazil’s government announced an online betting ban on Friday 25 September in São Paulo, nine days before the election. It outlaws online casino games and bets on real sporting events alike.

The tool is a provisional measure (medida provisória): a presidential decree with the force of law from the day it is published. Congress must approve it within 120 days, or it lapses.

Brazil Bans Online Betting: Deposits Stop, Sites Go Dark on 6 October

What the government announced

Finance Minister Dario Durigan set out the timetable at the event. “From today, no more money can be put into betting sites in the country,” he said.

Sites stay open only so that bettors can withdraw what is left, until 23:59 Brasília time on Monday 5 October. From midnight on 6 October, app stores, internet providers and Brazil’s internet steering committee must block the sites and apps, g1 reported.

Operators must report each customer’s balance to their banks on 7 and 8 October. Banks then return unclaimed money in full between 9 and 14 October, and state bank Caixa steps in where that fails.

All betting advertising, online and offline, must come down by 23:59 on 5 October, as must sponsors’ brands. No new betting ads are allowed once the measure is published.

The measure was expected in an extra edition of the official gazette, the Diário Oficial da União, on Friday night. It had not appeared there by 22:00 GMT (19:00 in Brasília).

Crimes cannot be created by provisional measure under Brazil’s constitution, so a separate bill goes to Congress. Its draft sets four to six years in prison for operating fixed-odds betting, even with a foreign licence, g1 reported.

The draft adds two to four years for betting advertising, for selling personal data to target bettors and for processing betting payments knowingly. Journalistic, educational and critical content is exempt.

A US$7 billion market, licensed for under two years

Brazil legalised fixed-odds betting in December 2018, under President Michel Temer. Rules came only with a 2023 law signed by Lula, and the licensed market opened on 1 January 2025.

Each company paid R$30 million (about US$5.8 million) for a five-year licence. Some 85 companies hold one, running nearly 190 brands on websites ending in .bet.br.

In 2025 those sites kept R$36.96 billion (about US$7.1 billion) after paying out prizes, the finance ministry’s betting secretariat reports. That measure, gross gaming revenue, is in effect what Brazilian bettors lost.

The secretariat counted 25.2 million individual bettors, roughly one Brazilian adult in six. Online casino games, not football, bring in 70 to 80 percent of operators’ revenue, by industry estimates cited in Estadão.

The federal tax agency collected about R$9.95 billion (about US$1.9 billion) from betting firms in 2025. That includes a 12 percent levy on revenue, worth R$4.5 billion (about US$870 million), split among sport, tourism, security and other areas.

Dollar conversions use 5.175 reais per US dollar, the open.er-api.com rate on 25 September 2026.

Finance Minister Dario Durigan says the money will not decide the matter. “If it harms the people, the revenue is not justified,” he told the weekly CartaCapital.

Why Lula wants betting gone

Lula ties betting to household debt, which polls cite as one reason for his government’s low approval. Central Bank data show debt payments took a record 28.9 percent of household income in June.

That series began in 2011, and June’s reading is its highest. A Central Bank director said in early September that betting platforms are a “central element” in that squeeze, Folha reported.

Public alarm grew in 2024, when a Central Bank study looked at Bolsa Família, Brazil’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families. It found five million people in recipient families sent betting sites R$3 billion (about US$580 million) in August.

That equalled about a fifth of the programme’s payments that month. The federal audit court later warned that the study could not show the money came from the benefit itself.

“I discovered that betting is a disease,” Lula told a rally in Maceió on Thursday night. “I am going to end these bets before they end Brazil.”

At a rally in Guarulhos on 18 September, he said the state could live without the tax. “What I cannot lose is the lives of the poor who gamble,” he added, InfoMoney reported.

State finance secretaries’ committee Comsefaz, with the Celso Furtado centre (Cicef), estimates that bettors lost a net R$62.5 billion (about US$12.1 billion) in 2025. The industry disputes the method and points to the official R$37 billion.

Economists at the University of São Paulo’s Made research centre go further. Using Cicef data, they estimate that betting drained R$120 billion to R$141 billion (about US$23 billion to US$27 billion) from economic activity in 2025, Gazeta do Povo and Times Brasil reported.

That is 0.9 to 1.1 percent of GDP, by their count, because money lost to betting was not spent on goods and services. It is a model estimate that includes knock-on effects on spending, not a count of money bettors lost.

An election nine days away

The ban comes nine days before the first round of the presidential election, on Sunday 4 October. Lula is seeking a fourth term; his main rival is Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the right-wing Liberal Party.

An Atlas/Bloomberg poll published on 23 September found 75 percent of Brazilians think online betting should be banned, Exame reported. Lula’s campaign now uses the slogan “Flávio é bet, Lula é o caminho” — “Flávio is a bet, Lula is the way.”

There is an irony. The licensing system Lula now wants to scrap was built by his own finance ministry, then led by Fernando Haddad.

He first floated a ban in October 2024, reported at the time as Brazil’s President Considers Online Betting Ban if Regulation Fails. Cities are moving too, as in Betting Advertising Ban Clears First Vote in São Paulo.

Industry and football push back

Nine industry associations issued a manifesto on Thursday titled “We Bet on Brazil.” They argue a ban would push players to illegal sites with no ID checks, no self-exclusion and no block on welfare recipients.

After the announcement, the Brazilian Institute for Responsible Gaming (IBJR), the National Gaming and Lotteries Association (ANJL) and licensed operators replied with a statement titled “To ban is not to protect”. Citing the finance ministry, they say 31 million people are active on licensed sites, and that unlicensed sites already take 41 percent of all money wagered.

Carlos Lima, who heads the IBJR, said operators will sue to recover licence fees and investments. The IBJR says its members hold 70 percent of the market.

Industry groups estimate that compensation claims against the state could reach R$120 billion (about US$23 billion). The figure is preliminary and not official.

More than half of the 20 top-flight football clubs have a betting firm as main shirt sponsor. Betting sponsors paid those clubs more than R$1 billion (over US$190 million) in 2025.

Sponsors including Betano, which backs Flamengo, have told clubs their contracts end automatically once the measure is issued, radio network CBN reported. Aides say help for clubs, such as cheaper credit, will likely come after the election.

Lula has brushed the warnings aside. “This is not a war, it is a decision,” he said at a campaign event in Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday.

His rival Flávio Bolsonaro called the move “populist, hypocritical and electioneering”, Poder360 reported. He said that, if elected, he would ban online casino games such as “Tigrinho” (Fortune Tiger), a popular slot game, but signalled he would keep sports betting, g1 reported.

What comes next

The key dates for bettors are 5 October, the last day to withdraw, and 6 October, when sites go dark. Election day, Sunday 4 October, falls the day before the withdrawal deadline.

Once published, the measure has the force of law at once. Congress has 60 days to vote, extendable by 60 more, and the count pauses during its year-end recess.

A final vote could therefore run into early 2027. Lawmakers can approve it, amend it — for example to keep sports betting — or let it lapse.

Court challenges are near certain. Operators say they will sue to recover licence fees and investments, and the criminal bill still needs Congress.

Nor does the ban end illegal betting, which the authorities already fight site by site. More than 25,000 illegal betting sites were blocked between October 2024 and December 2025.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the online betting ban already in force?

Not yet. It was announced on 25 September and takes effect when published in the official gazette, expected in an extra edition that night; deposits stop from publication.

What is a provisional measure?

It is a decree the Brazilian president can issue in urgent cases, with the force of law from publication. Congress must approve it within 120 days, not counting its recess, or it lapses.

Does it cover sports betting or only online casinos?

Both. The government says the ban covers online casino games and fixed-odds bets on real sporting events.

What happens to money bettors hold on licensed sites?

Bettors can withdraw until 23:59 on 5 October. Unclaimed balances are returned through the operators’ banks between 9 and 14 October, with Caixa handling cases that fail.

Sources: Finance Minister Dario Durigan and g1, announcement of 25 September 2026; g1, industry statement and Comsefaz/Cicef estimate, 25 September 2026; Poder360 and g1, Flávio Bolsonaro reaction, 25 September 2026; Gazeta do Povo and Times Brasil, Made/FEA-USP estimate, 25 September 2026; Estadão, O Globo, Folha de S.Paulo, CNN Brasil, UOL, Valor Econômico, Exame, JOTA, CBN, InfoMoney, Poder360 and CartaCapital, reports of 23–25 September 2026; Ministry of Finance, Secretariat of Prizes and Bets, 2025 market panorama; Federal Revenue Service, 2025 collection data; Central Bank of Brazil, Technical Note 513/2024 and household credit statistics for June 2026; Federal Court of Accounts (TCU), Ruling 2529/2025; exchange rate from open.er-api.com, 25 September 2026.

World.title: Quickmart Kenya Grows on Supplier Credit Rather Than Bank Debt
World.content:
KENYA · RETAIL

Key Facts — The country Kenya’s formal retail sector has seen several large chains fail under debt in the past decade.

— The model Quickmart funds new stores mainly from internally generated cash, with suppliers carrying stock.

— The scale It runs 72 stores across 16 counties, 35 of them open around the clock.

— The money Revenue was 50.4 billion shillings in 2025, about US$389 million.

— The catch The proposed listing has no regulatory approval and no published offer price.

Quickmart Kenya opens ten to fifteen stores a year without borrowing much. Its suppliers carry the stock.

Nairobi. Kenyan retail has seen several large chains fail under debt. (Photo: Yahya, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Quickmart Kenya has set out how it pays for growth, ahead of a proposed Nairobi listing. The answer is internal cash and supplier credit rather than bank debt.

How Quickmart Kenya pays for new stores

The chain opens between ten and fifteen stores a year. It says that expansion is funded primarily through internally generated cash.

The second source is its suppliers. They finance stock and working capital in place of bank borrowing.

That is a specific and narrow claim. It is about how inventory is carried, not about growth being free.

More than 700 suppliers deal with the chain. Direct delivery and trade terms keep the capital requirement down.

It is a common model in grocery retail worldwide. What varies is how long the retailer takes to pay.

Why the model matters in Kenya

Kenyan retail has a history of failure. Nakumatt and Tuskys both went under after expanding on debt and delaying supplier payments.

In both cases suppliers were the unsecured creditors who lost most. That memory shapes how the sector reads any growth story.

So a chain that says suppliers fund its stock is making a claim that cuts two ways. It is efficient, and it concentrates risk on the same people.

The company says it pays on time. That assertion is central to the model and has not been independently verified.

Anyone weighing the business should want evidence on it. Payment terms are the difference between efficiency and a squeeze.

The numbers behind it

Revenue in 2025 was 50.4 billion shillings, about US$389 million. Adjusted profit after tax was 1.7 billion shillings, about US$13 million.

The statutory figure is lower. Reported net profit was 1.51 billion shillings, about US$11.7 million.

First-half revenue in 2026 reached 27.3 billion shillings, about US$211 million. That is ahead of the same period last year.

The chain employs more than 8,000 people. It handles roughly 5 million customer transactions a month.

Its stated target is more than 100 stores. That is a further 30 or so at the current pace.

What the listing would actually do

The seller is not Quickmart itself. It is Sokoni Retail Kenya, the sole shareholder, which is controlled by the Mauritius-based Adenia Partners.

Sokoni proposes to sell 2 billion existing shares, half of the 4 billion issued. No new capital would be raised for the business.

An over-allotment of up to 15 percent could reduce Sokoni’s remaining holding to about 42.5 percent. The listed entity would be Quick Mart PLC.

This is a private equity exit rather than a fundraising. That distinction changes what the proceeds are for.

Nothing is approved yet

Neither the Capital Markets Authority nor the Nairobi Securities Exchange has approved the offer. No offer price has been published.

The company has said the offer is expected to open around the end of September 2026. That timing has not been confirmed by the regulator.

Reported valuation talk has ranged from 25.5 billion to 34 billion shillings, about US$197 million to US$263 million. Those are estimates, not a price.

Until a prospectus is approved, none of this is investable. It is an intention to float.

We reported the same caution on 24 September. Nothing has changed since on the approval.

What it would mean for Kenyan investors

The Nairobi exchange has had few large new listings in a decade. A retailer of this size would be a notable addition.

Quickmart has indicated a dividend payout target of about 80 percent of earnings. It has suggested a first dividend in the first half of 2027.

For ordinary savers, the appeal is a business they use rather than one they read about. That is rare on the exchange.

The risk is the same as the model. A chain that leans on supplier credit is exposed if those terms tighten.

What is not yet known

The offer price is unknown. So is the final size, after any over-allotment.

No regulatory approval has been granted. The timetable depends on it.

The company’s payment terms with suppliers have not been published. That detail is the model’s load-bearing wall.

Whether Adenia intends to sell further down after listing is also unstated. Its remaining stake would be substantial.

FAQ

How does Quickmart Kenya fund its growth?

Mainly from internally generated cash, with suppliers financing stock and working capital rather than banks. It opens ten to fifteen stores a year.

Who is selling shares in the proposed listing?

Sokoni Retail Kenya, the sole shareholder, controlled by Adenia Partners. It proposes to sell 2 billion existing shares, half the company.

Has the listing been approved?

No. Neither the Capital Markets Authority nor the Nairobi Securities Exchange has approved it, and no offer price has been published.

How big is Quickmart?

It runs 72 stores across 16 counties, 35 of them open around the clock, and employs more than 8,000 people. Revenue was about US$389 million in 2025.

Sources: Business Daily on the growth model; Eastleigh Voice and The Star on the proposed listing; Capital FM on the financial figures.

World.title: Nigeria Motor Insurance May Shift to Third-Party Cover, an Insurer Says
World.content:
NIGERIA · FINANCE

Key Facts — The country Nigeria has about 220 million people and one of Africa’s largest but thinnest insurance markets.

— What was said An insurance executive expects more drivers to choose third-party cover over comprehensive policies.

— The status This is a stated expectation, not a measured change in the market.

— The money The minimum third-party premium is 15,000 naira a year, about US$11.

— The catch Comprehensive cover starts at 5 percent of a vehicle’s value, a different order of cost.

Nigeria motor insurance has not visibly shifted. This is one insurer’s prediction, and the gap between the two policies is the point.

Lagos traffic. Third-party motor cover is compulsory in Nigeria and costs about US1 a year. (Photo: satanoid from Austin, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

An executive at a Nigerian insurer expects rising fuel and running costs to push drivers toward cheaper cover. Nigeria motor insurance already sits at prices that look small in dollar terms.

What was actually said

Katherine Itua is executive director for finance and investments at Consolidated Hallmark Insurance. She made the comment in September 2026.

As fuel and vehicle running costs rise, she said, more customers are likely to choose third-party cover. It is more affordable than comprehensive.

That is a forecast about customer behaviour. No data showing an actual shift has been published.

It is worth stating clearly because the distinction is easy to lose. An expectation is not a trend.

What Nigeria motor insurance costs

Third-party cover pays for damage to other people. The regulator sets a minimum premium of 15,000 naira a year, about US$11.

That minimum has applied since 1 January 2023, when it rose from 5,000 naira, about US$4. The increase was 200 percent.

Comprehensive cover also pays for the owner’s own vehicle. The regulator sets a minimum of 5 percent of the sum insured.

On a car insured for 3 million naira, about US$2,260, that is roughly 150,000 naira, about US$113. The gap between the two is the whole argument.

The costs pressing on insurers

Insurers face the same fuel bills as their customers. Offices, field operations, claims work and sales networks all run on fuel and generators.

Consolidated Hallmark budgeted petrol at about 1,500 naira a litre for 2026, roughly US$1.13. It budgeted diesel at about 2,000 naira, roughly US$1.51.

Those are planning assumptions rather than pump prices. They indicate what the company expects to pay.

Higher running costs squeeze margins on low-value policies hardest. Third-party business is the lowest-value line there is.

That cuts against the prediction rather than supporting it. A shift to cheaper policies would thin insurers’ margins further.

What the rules now require

Third-party motor cover is compulsory in Nigeria. The obligation comes from motor vehicle legislation rather than from a regulator’s statement.

The minimum third-party property damage limit for a private car is 3 million naira, about US$2,260. That figure rose with the 2023 premium change.

A larger reform has since arrived. The Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act was signed on 6 August 2025 and took effect the same day.

It sets a 60-day deadline for settling admitted claims, with interest penalties for late payment. It also creates a compensation fund for road accident victims.

Why enforcement is the real variable

The regulatory minimum and the market price are not the same thing. Some insurers and comparison sites still advertise cover from 5,000 naira, about US$4.

That gap tells you how patchy enforcement is. A minimum price that is widely undercut is a target rather than a rule.

The reform act ties valid cover to a national insurance database. In principle that makes undercutting harder to hide.

In practice, the change will show in claims data rather than in announcements. That will take a year or more.

Until then, the published minimum and the advertised price will keep diverging. Buyers should read the cover, not the headline rate.

What this means for drivers

For a driver on a tight budget, third-party cover is the legal minimum and the cheap option. It pays nothing toward your own car.

At about US$11 a year it is inexpensive by any international measure. At about US$113, so is comprehensive cover.

The real constraint is income rather than the premium. That is why the executive’s prediction is plausible even without data behind it.

Anyone comparing quotes should check the property damage limit. Below 3 million naira, about US$2,260, the policy does not meet the minimum.

What is not yet known

No figures show an actual move from comprehensive to third-party cover. Only one executive’s expectation has been reported.

Policy volume data by class has not been published for 2026. Without it the claim cannot be tested.

The current pump price of petrol was not stated alongside the comment. Only the company’s budget assumption is on record.

How the regulator will enforce the reform act’s provisions is also unclear. No enforcement actions have been announced.

FAQ

Is Nigeria motor insurance shifting to third-party cover?

One insurance executive expects it to. No published data shows an actual shift in policy purchases.

How much is third-party motor cover in Nigeria?

The regulatory minimum is 15,000 naira a year, about US$11. Some insurers still advertise cover from 5,000 naira, about US$4.

What does comprehensive cover cost?

The regulator sets a minimum of 5 percent of the sum insured. On a car insured for 3 million naira, that is about 150,000 naira, roughly US$113.

What changed in the 2025 reform act?

It set a 60-day deadline for settling admitted claims, with interest penalties for late payment. It also created a road accident victims fund and tied valid cover to a national database.

Sources: Nairametrics on the executive’s remarks and on the 2023 premium change; SHQ Legal on the 2025 reform act; Proshare on the premium rates.

World.title: Rwanda AI Hub Takes Its Health and Farming Pitch to the UN
World.content:
RWANDA · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts — The country Rwanda has built its economic pitch on services and technology rather than on resources.

— What happened The ICT ministry hosted a session on deploying AI at scale, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

— The money The Gates Foundation committed about US$7.4 million over 34 months to the hub in November 2025.

— The tools A Kinyarwanda voice assistant called Tunga is being tested through an agriculture call centre.

— The catch Figures of US$17.5 million circulate widely but appear in no official statement.

The Rwanda AI hub is real and funded. The figures attached to it in circulation are not the ones in the grant record.

Kigali. Rwanda has positioned itself as the region’s test bed for new technology. (Photo: Dushime rw, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Rwanda’s ICT ministry hosted a session on artificial intelligence on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The Rwanda AI hub was set up in 2025 with Gates Foundation money and is now being shown abroad.

What the Rwanda AI hub is

The hub was announced at the Global AI Summit on Africa in Kigali on 4 April 2025. The partners are the government, the Gates Foundation and Rwanda’s Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

Paula Ingabire, the minister of ICT and innovation, signed for Rwanda. Trevor Mundel, the Gates Foundation’s president of global health, signed for the foundation.

The memorandum spoke of up to US$7.5 million over three years. It covers health, agriculture and education.

The foundation’s own grants record shows the committed figure. It is US$7.4 million over 34 months, committed in November 2025.

That is a real programme at a modest size. It is not the figure most coverage carries.

Where the larger numbers come from

A figure of US$17.5 million appears across technology sites and aggregators. It also appears as 25 billion Rwandan francs.

Neither number appears in a Gates Foundation, ministry or centre statement that we could find. That is worth saying plainly.

The nearest sourced claim is from Yves Iradukunda, a minister of state. In October 2025 he said the budget had more than doubled, to over US$15 million.

So the programme may well be larger than the single grant. The precise total has not been published.

The distinction matters for anyone sizing the effort. One grant is documented, and the rest is assertion.

What is actually running

Tunga is a voice assistant that works in Kinyarwanda. It answers farmers’ questions on crops, pests, fertiliser and markets.

It is in testing rather than deployment. In trials it answered about 60 percent of questions correctly, passing the rest to human experts.

The agriculture ministry and its partners built the knowledge base behind it. Ingabire presented the work at the Africa Food Systems Forum in Kigali in September 2026.

A 60 percent accuracy rate is not a finished product. It is a reasonable start for a service that escalates what it cannot answer.

The ministry runs the call centre behind it. Human advisers still take the remaining four questions in ten.

The health side of the programme

A separate initiative is larger. Horizon 1000 was announced on 20 January 2026 by OpenAI and the Gates Foundation.

It commits US$50 million to bring AI tools to 1,000 primary healthcare clinics by 2028. Rwanda is the first country.

That is roughly seven times the hub’s own grant. It also runs on a different timetable.

The two are related but not the same programme. Conflating them is how the larger figures enter circulation.

Why Rwanda gets these pilots

Rwanda has spent fifteen years positioning itself as the region’s test bed for technology. Drone delivery and digital identity both started there.

The country is small enough to cover and centralised enough to decide quickly. Those are the qualities pilot programmes look for.

The trade-off is scale. A tool that works across Rwanda’s 14 million people has not been proven across Nigeria’s 220 million.

Bill Gates met President Paul Kagame in July 2026 to discuss health, AI and agriculture. The relationship is long-running.

What it means on the ground

For farmers, the practical question is whether a call to the advisory line gets a useful answer. That is what Tunga is being tested against.

For patients, nothing has changed yet. Clinic deployments under Horizon 1000 run to 2028.

For investors, Rwanda’s value here is as a demonstration market rather than a large one. That is the honest reading.

The government’s aim is to be where these tools are proven. Proving them is not the same as owning them.

What is not yet known

The total programme budget has not been published. Only the single Gates grant figure is on the record.

No deployment timetable for Tunga has been announced. It remains in testing through the call centre.

How many farmers or clinics have been reached so far is unstated. No progress figures have been released.

Nor is it clear what happens when the 34-month grant ends. No successor funding has been announced.

FAQ

How much money is behind the Rwanda AI hub?

The Gates Foundation committed about US$7.4 million over 34 months in November 2025. A minister has separately said the wider budget exceeds US$15 million.

What is Tunga?

A Kinyarwanda-language voice assistant for farmers, covering crops, pests, fertiliser and markets. It is in testing and answered about 60 percent of trial questions correctly.

Who runs the hub?

The Rwandan government with the Gates Foundation and Rwanda’s Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution. It was announced in Kigali in April 2025.

What is Horizon 1000?

A separate US$50 million programme from OpenAI and the Gates Foundation to bring AI tools to 1,000 primary healthcare clinics by 2028. Rwanda is the first country.

Sources: Gates Foundation committed-grants record; Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Rwanda; OpenAI on Horizon 1000; KT Press on the agriculture plan.

World.title: Volta Economic Forum in Ghana Asks Investors for Signatures, Not Speeches
World.content:
GHANA · INVESTMENT

Key Facts — The country Ghana’s Volta Region borders Togo and holds the country’s largest lake and part of its coast.

— What happened The Volta Economic Forum convened in Ho on 23 September 2026, during the Asogli Te Za festival.

— The theme Organisers billed it as moving from opportunity showcase to investment execution.

— The record Five projects are attributed to the maiden forum, held at Whuti in November 2025.

— The catch No deal book, financing timetable or progress report has been published.

The Volta Economic Forum’s own theme was execution. Its organisers say the region has had enough showcases.

Ghana’s Volta Region, where the forum met, is underweight in the country’s investment map. (Photo: Celestinesucess, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
