World.title: 'It's an absolute Ferrari to fly on': ADF retires attack helicopters
World.content:
After more than two decades, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) is farewelling its $1.1-billion fleet of attack helicopters, known as the Tigers, and replacing them with American Apaches.

The Tiger Armed Reconnaissance Helicopters (ARH) will be retired from use in the ADF this month, and the 1st Aviation Regiment will be transitioned to Townsville away from Darwin.

Nicholas Bilton described flying the Tigers as a childhood dream come true. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Captain Nicholas Bilton, who is based in Darwin and has been flying the Tigers for three years, said the experience has been "absolutely awesome".

"It's literally me living out my childhood dream — I've wanted to do it ever since I was a kid," he said.

"I think I'll just savour the moment, enjoy the memories Tiger brought.

"I really enjoyed flying it but I'm ready for the next steps."

Known for their speed and agility, the 22 Tiger ARHs were acquired by the Australian defence force in 2001 and have been in service since 2004.

Tiger ARHs have been used by the Australian Defence force for more than 20 years. (Supplied: Australian Defence Force)

According to a 2016 report, Australia was one of four countries operating the two-seater attack helicopters, with France, Germany and Spain also including them in their fleets.

It's unknown yet where the Tigers will be retired to, although last year the Albanese government considered offloading them to Kyiv to aid in Ukraine's war efforts

Captain Bilton last week completed a final send off for the Tigers with a flyover of the iconic Mindil Beach Markets.

"I'm going to miss most of the manoeuvrability of the Tiger — it's an absolute Ferrari to fly on … I'm going to miss it," he said.

From Tigers to Apaches

Lieutenant-Colonel Jason Perrins said the Tigers have been a "key and longstanding" part of the unit.

"It's been part of the furniture here really, and all of the people that have been through it, it is going to be a sad time but it's also been an excellent period through that and we're celebrating the people," he said.

Jason Perrins was one of the first to be qualified to fly the Apache helicopter. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

He said the Tigers have participated in international exercises, supporting the US and recently showing off defence capabilities to international partners in Malaysia.

The regiment's aircraft will be transitioned to AH‑64E Apache attack helicopters, which are being acquired from the United States in a $4.5 billion dollar deal.

Six Apaches have been delivered to Townsville, with all 29 expected to arrive in Australia by the end of 2029.

The Australian Army has acquired 29 new AH-64E Apache attack helicopters. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Lieutenant-Colonel Perrins was one of the first army pilots qualified to fly the Apaches.

"I wouldn't say the Tigers can't keep up, both are excellent attack platforms, but what the Apache does, it is a step-up in a number of areas, connectivity and data systems and sensors," he said.

An ADF spokesperson said the transition to the Apache Helicopter reflected "Australia's need to operate in an evolving threat environment".

World.title: Fake TV police station fuels outback town's plea for real thing
World.content:
For three days this year, locals in the historic main street of Boulder, in Western Australia's Goldfields, got a glimpse of what it would be like with a police station back in town.

There was just one problem — the station was not real.

Boulder's heritage-listed courthouse had been transformed into a fictional police station for the upcoming Stan crime series Two Birds, which has been filming in the region.

While it was just set dressing, Ronnie and Stephen Maddocks, who run the neighbouring Grand Hotel, said the change on Burt Street was almost immediate.

"Everything went dead quiet for about three days until they realised it wasn't a real police station," Ms Maddocks said.

While the set has since been dismantled, locals want fiction to become fact, with calls growing for a permanent police presence to return.

Home to shops and a number of historic pubs, Boulder's main street has also been a magnet for crime and antisocial behaviour.

Grand Hotel Boulder owners Stephen and Ronnie Maddocks signed the petition for a police post in Boulder. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

Just last weekend, a worker at one of the licensed premises was allegedly threatened with a hammer, after trying to stop someone stealing cash and alcohol.

Mr Maddocks said he once had a knife pulled on him while waiting with a customer for a taxi.

He said customers at the Grand had also been attacked when leaving.

This statue of a miner on Burt Street is a tribute to the workers who gave the golden mile its worldwide reputation. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

Their concerns are shared by more than 1,000 people who have signed a petition calling for a 24-hour shopfront police station on Burt Street.

Historic street struggling for confidence

Boulder and neighbouring Kalgoorlie developed as separate towns before amalgamating in 1989, but retain separate and distinctive identities.

In a decade behind the counter, Boulder Newsagency owner Mike Saville said he has watched visitor numbers steadily decline.

An archival photo of Boulder city around 1911. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

Mr Saville said theft and verbal abuse had become a daily problem, and more foot patrols from police could help.

Mike Saville has owned Boulder Newsagency and Lotto for 10 years. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

"Police presence should be walking up and down the street," he said.

"Not all day long every day, but up and down the street for an hour in the morning, an hour in the afternoon, so people see them."

The Maddocks have noticed more police vehicles and occasional foot patrols since the campaign for a permanent presence began.

"When that's happening, everything goes a little bit quieter," Ms Maddocks said.

Kalgoorlie's super pit can be seen from the top of Burt Street in Boulder. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

She acknowledged a police post alone would not address all of the issues facing the area.

"I think it would be a good start trying to breathe a bit of life back into the place," she said.

"Because if people don't feel comfortable going to the shops, they're not going to come."

Police point to existing patrols

Kalgoorlie Police Station sits about 5 kilometres from Burt Street, with WA Police saying officers respond to calls across Kalgoorlie-Boulder 24 hours a day and regularly patrol Boulder.

Operation Regional Shield was extended to the Goldfields in 2024, bringing more police officers and law enforcement resources to the region to address escalating concerns about anti-social behaviour.

Police would not disclose the current staffing levels, but said resources were continually assessed and allocated based on operational demand and community safety needs.

WA Police say officers routinely patrol and respond to incidents in Boulder from Kalgoorlie Police Station. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

WA Police data shows 1,742 offences were recorded in Boulder in 2025, up from 1,515 in 2024.

Within the first six months of this year, 1,141 offences had already been recorded.

'Feet on the street'

The local campaign has the support of Dave Grills, a former Kalgoorlie-Boulder police officer who walked the beat on Burt Street, prior to the closure of the previous post.

The post was a replacement for the former Boulder Police Station, which closed in the early 1990s.

He later served as an Upper House MP for the WA Nationals, sat on the Kalgoorlie-Boulder City council and is currently a councillor at the Shire of Mundaring in the Perth Hills.

"To have that presence down there is the thing that's needed, it's how the police will do it with the resources they have," he said.

" Until you have a police officer there in a uniform working face-to-face with people, you won't fix the problem. "

A number of buildings on Burt Street are damaged, many of them boarded up. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

He said he tried unsuccessfully to have the shopfront retained after being told it could no longer be resourced.

The petition to reopen the post, signed by 1,171 people, was tabled in WA Parliament on September 10 by Liberal MP Neil Thomson.

Mr Thomson said retailers had raised concerns with him about theft, drug use and worker safety.

"They share the immense frustration about crime and antisocial behaviour in the town retail precinct," he said.

"The most troubling aspect is the constant fear of assault retail workers have, whether they be minor or major assaults."

World.title: Sailor, 75, on his last legs and last beer when help arrived
World.content:
After a freak wave off the coast of Timor-Leste in July destroyed Digby Campbell's navigational equipment and much of his rations, what was supposed to be a six-day voyage to Darwin turned into a weeks-long ordeal.

The 75-year-old veteran sailor was found drifting in Darwin Harbour last month, sunburnt, dehydrated and disoriented aboard his trimaran the Singapore Sling, more than a month after he departed Dili in early July.

Maritime officer Chris Chridland was one of the three men who spotted the boat and approached to do a welfare check.

"It just looked tired, so we thought we'd better go and have a look," he said.

Digby Campbell had been standing at the Singapore Sling's helm for a day and a half when he was finally rescued. (Supplied: Joshua Witkin)

Launch master Rawson McCrae and crew member Joshua Witkin said the Singapore Sling and its captain were in a sorry state when they pulled up alongside it.

"I said, 'You alright mate?' And he said, 'Not really,'" Mr Witkin said.

Mr McCrae said Mr Campbell's ankles were "swollen like you would not believe".

The men learned Mr Campbell had been standing at the yacht's helm trying to steer the ship into port for a day and a half and had not eaten for three days.

Rawson McCrae says he later realised he had sailed on the decades-old trimaran himself as a 10-year-old boy. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

"I was buggered," Mr Campbell said.

The trio helped Mr Campbell safely to shore and into a waiting ambulance, but not before they had organised to meet again for a beer, to hear the full tale of the Singapore Sling's voyage.

"He said, 'I wanted to make a Sunday sesh, it's what kept me going,'" Mr McCrae said.

" We said, 'We'll have one with you mate, you're a legend.' "

An angry harbourmaster, two backpackers and a pushbike

Mr Campbell said he had flown from Bundaberg to Dili in June to purchase the Singapore Sling, knowing the Val 31 trimaran to be a reliable vessel.

But he was held up in Dili, awaiting the handover of the boat's registration in the harbourmaster's office shortly before it closed for the day.

"All of a sudden [the harbourmaster] said, 'We gotta wait for someone,'" Mr Campbell said.

"Next minute this French backpacker shows up. He said, 'I want you to take this man with you.'

"Another French backpacker comes in and he's got a pushbike."

The view from the Singapore Sling before Digby Campbell left Dili, without the two backpackers. (Supplied: Digby Campbell)

Mr Campbell said he was able to convince the harbourmaster that the boat was not equipped for three passengers and was also in worse shape than he had expected.

"He was angry but he gave me my stamp and away I went," he said.

Two days out of port in early July, the Singapore Sling ran into rough seas off Timor's east coast and began falling apart.

"The big outboard on the back broke part of the bracket away and went underwater," Mr Campbell said.

"And about the same time one chain plate broke — that holds the mast up — and the battens were flying out of the main.

"So I had a motor in the water, the headsail was tangled up, and then another big wave come up over the back and took out the tablet and my phone."

Christopher Cridland says it would have taken Mr Campbell another two days to reach the harbour if he had not been rescued. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

Faced with a choice between returning to Dili and pushing on to Darwin, Mr Campbell said he was only really left with one option.

"I thought the smart thing to do was turn around and go back, but I couldn't — I got the port captain and these two French backpackers on a pushbike. There was no way I was going back," he said.

At that point Mr Campbell had given Australian authorities four days' notice of his expected arrival into Darwin for what he thought was a six-day voyage.

During what turned into a four-week trip, Mr Campbell said he was given supplies and radio equipment by Australian Border Force personnel and received a welfare check in the dead of night from a Royal Australian Navy warship.

"I said, 'Convey my thanks to the captain, I'm OK,'" he said.

But by the time he reached Australian waters Mr Campbell's supplies were running dangerously low.

The Singapore Sling is now being prepared in Darwin for its next journey to New Zealand with a fresh coat of paint. (Supplied: Digby Campbell)

"I had one can of beer and two cans of Red Bull," he said.

"I thought, 'When I see Australia, I'm going to have that can of beer.'

"I actually drank the can of beer when I saw the lights of Darwin. I never saw land, but I thought, 'There's land there under the light.'"

Mr Cridland said when Mr Campbell was eventually rescued in waters off Darwin Harbour there was barely any wind and that his boat was only moving at about 1.5 knots per hour.

"It would've taken him two days to get into harbour with wind like that," he said.

An unexpected connection

When Mr Campbell was able to reunite with his three rescuers after recovering from the harrowing journey, one of them discovered he had his own connection to the Singapore Sling.

"We were able to make contact and caught up at Dinah Beach for a beer [and] started hearing Digby's stories," Mr McCrae said.

Joshua Witkin, Rawson McCrae and Christopher Cridland were presented with Distinguished Lifesaving Awards in Darwin this week. (Supplied: AMOU)

Having grown up in Darwin's sailing community, Mr McCrae said a nagging feeling led him to ask about the Singapore Sling's previous owner and realised he had actually sailed on the decades-old trimaran himself as a 10-year-old boy.

"Wow! This is freaky," he said.

Solo sailor rescued from sinking yacht Navy, AMSA personnel winched the Canadian sailor to safety after his vessel began taking on water 1,000 kilometres south-east of Christmas Island.

For their heroics, Mr McCrae, Mr Witkin and Mr Cridland were each given Distinguished Lifesaving Awards from the Australian Maritime Officers Union (AMOU) at an informal presentation at a pub on Darwin's waterfront this week.

"Their actions embody the very best traditions of the maritime profession and serve as a reminder that mariners look after one another, whether they are colleagues or complete strangers," AMOU president Matthew Jepsen said in a statement.

With the Singapore Sling repaired and given a fresh coat of paint, Mr Campbell said he was preparing to set sail for New Zealand, via Cairns, in a couple of weeks.

"I'll just wait for the wind to get the right direction," he said.

World.title: Serial con man turned charity director back in court on dishonesty charges
World.content:
A serial con man, who impersonated a police officer before turning his life around to head up a charity, is back in court on dishonesty charges.

Second Chances director Samuel Mark Narroway has been charged with two counts of dishonest dealings with documents and two counts of being unlawfully on premises — all alleged to have occurred last December at Mobilong, Murray Bridge and Northfield.

Shane Sanchez, representing Mr Narroway, told the Elizabeth Magistrates Court this week "they are contested charges at this point in time".

The case was adjourned until November.

Mr Narroway, who appeared in court wearing a shirt bearing the Second Chances logo, made no comment as he left.

Second Chances vice-chair Leslie Dennis confirmed the latest charges are linked to Mr Narroway's role at the charity but said management remained supportive.

"I have a deep respect for Sam and his work for the organisation and I pray that there is no proof in the accusations made against him," he said.

" He's still involved [in Second Chances] and we're supporting him … we trust that he won't be found guilty. "

Samuel Narroway became the director of Second Chances after serving six years in prison. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

The charity Second Chances, which helps prisoners and their children, had its funding cut by the state government after the charges were laid.

History of impersonating officials

Mr Narroway has a long history of fraud offending, including a conviction for impersonating a police officer three times in a 24-hour period in 2019.

Using a fake badge and a car with flashing red and blue lights, he and another man pulled over victims and forced one driver to pay a bogus fine.

In 2016, Mr Narroway was fined for posing as a SafeWork SA inspector and conducting phoney inspections at multiple businesses.

He told the ABC in November last year that he spent nearly six years behind bars, and became involved with Second Chances through a friendship with the charity's founders.

"People can change," he said at the time.

"People should be able to deserve a second chance."

Uncertain future for charity

In a media release last month, Mr Narroway said Second Chances was advised on August 6 that funding for its Family Support Service would "cease from 31 December 2026 due to budget constraints".

"This decision places at risk one of the few specialist services in South Australia dedicated to supporting children affected by parental imprisonment," he said.

"If government does not reverse this decision, Second Chances will need approximately $300,000 per year from the community or private sector to continue this work and ensure these children and families are not left out in the cold."

Second Chances runs a hub in suburban Adelaide that includes an op shop. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

Mr Narroway — who is at various points described as the organisation's director, secretary and general manager — made no mention of the charges against him.

Second Chances has launched an online petition and fundraiser, appealing for donations to keep the service running.

The office of Human Services Minister Katrine Hildyard did not respond to questions about why the government cut funding for Second Chances.

"[The Department of Human Services] has arrangements in place to ensure funded organisations meet contractual obligations," a government spokesperson said.

Prior to the cut, approximately $200,000 in annual government funding was provided to Second Chances.

World.title: Urgent dredging underway to save disappearing Queensland beach
World.content:
Dredging is underway to save a disappearing regional Queensland beach, but there are questions about its long-term viability and the impacts of increasingly powerful weather events.

At Moore Park Beach, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, 5 metres of the foreshore has washed away since Tropical Cyclone Alfred hit in early 2025.

Another major flood event in March this year exacerbated the situation.

The extent of the transformation is striking. The mouth of Moore Park Creek migrated about 200 metres north during the flood, prompting the Bundaberg Regional Council to take urgent action.

Council is relocating the creek mouth. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

Mayor Helen Blackburn said the council had been working with engineers to decide on appropriate measures.

"A dredge will be closing one part of the creek mouth and then opening up a different section to allow for the creek to create its own mouth a little further to the south," she said.

"This dredge will also take additional sand and nourish Moore Park Beach where the erosion has occurred."

Cr Blackburn said the appropriate government permits to carry out dredging work had been granted.

It is hoped the safety fencing will be removed in time for Christmas.

Geographer and Sunshine Coast University associate professor Javier Leon said the council needed to consider longer-term solutions for the community.

There are questions about whether dredging will work in the long term. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

"I think there needs to be short-term solutions that could include realigning the mouth, for example, but we also should be focusing on medium to long-term solutions because this is not stopping anytime soon. If anything, it might get worse as the decades go on," Dr Leon said.

"It's very site-specific. For example, a few years ago, the study came out looking at changes in the shoreline around Australia and it showed that 50 per cent are eroding and 50 per cent are accreting, so there's no consistent signal that we can take just yet."

Moore Park Beach Community Association president Derek Alcorn said the erosion had deterred visitors.

"The beach out at Moore Park Beach is the most precious thing we've got for tourists to come out there. It's a beautiful beach," Mr Alcorn said.

"Until they get it rectified, it's probably going to be a financial burden against the community."

Moore Park Beach is north of Bundaberg. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

In 2025, the council was required to demolish the former Moore Park Beach surf club because the building was slipping into the ocean.

Mr Alcorn said, apart from the development of a new surf club several hundred metres away from the old site, there were still two stages of the beachfront redevelopment to go ahead.

"They're on hold at the moment until they can get things stabilised, so there's a lot more benefit to come to the community once they fix the beach," he said.

Stephen Bennett and Helen Blackburn hold the coastal erosion plan. (Supplied: Stephen Bennett)

From a longer-term perspective, the council has been awarded almost $140,000 in state and federal funding to develop a shoreline erosion management plan.

Burnett MP Stephen Bennett said the plan required a staged approach.

"That is a strategic document that needs to continue to provide solutions going forward and better inform the council, the engineers and marine scientists about what we do to continue to provide solutions to the Moore Park Beach community," Mr Bennett said.

World.title: Retired doctor extradited from NSW pleads not guilty to indecent assault
World.content:
A patient who was allegedly indecently assaulted by his GP two decades ago has told a Tasmanian court that he was frightened of reporting the incident at the time.

The hearing for retired doctor Michael Anthony Welch, 65, was before the Hobart Magistrates Court on Friday.

Mr Welch practised as a GP in Tasmania from 1984 until his retirement in 2019.

Last year, he was extradited from New South Wales to face three indecent assault charges.

Mr Welch pleaded not guilty to the charges.

In his opening statement, prosecutor Adam Godleman said the first two charges related to a complainant who was allegedly assaulted twice during a consult in late 2004 or early 2005, when he was 18 or 19 years old.

Mr Welch has denied these allegations.

Complainant alleges he was 'frozen, eyes wide'

Mr Godleman said the first charge related to a groin assessment, where the complainant was standing and Mr Welch was seated, and the second charge involved the young man lying on the bed while his penis was assessed.

The complainant told the court that he went to Mr Welch because he was known as an LGBTQI+ friendly doctor.

"It was quite well known in the gay community that there was a gay doctor you could go to," he said.

He said the alleged assaults occurred when he attended for a "sexual health check-up".

The complainant described that when he stood up for the first examination, Mr Welch indecently touched his genitals over the top of his underwear and flicked the waistband.

He went on to say that when he was lying on the bed, Mr Welch allegedly began stroking his genitals.

"[I was] shocked … frozen, eyes quite wide," he said.

"He said to me, 'You're so cute, you're going to get me into trouble, I have to stop'."

The complainant said he didn't say or do anything while the allegations unfolded.

During the cross-examination by Mr Welch's lawyer, David Edwardson KC, the complainant was asked why he had waited until 2023 to report the incident to the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA).

"I was genuinely frightened," he said.

" I was very young. I did not think anyone would believe me. Who is going to believe an 18–19-year-old guy over a doctor? "

Doctor denies allegations

During his evidence, Mr Welch denied the allegations and denied making any inappropriate comments.

Mr Welch said the complainant had asked for a sexual health examination, which he provided in a professional way.

"It was all within [the] constraints of a normal examination," he said.

He said he had no sexual interest in the complainant and was not attracted to him.

He said that during the examination on the bed, he was looking at the complainant to gauge whether he was in pain or discomfort.

"If someone felt like they were not happy with the outcome, they would feel comfortable to raise that," he told the court.

The complainant told the court Mr Welch was well known as an LGBTQI+ friendly doctor. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

In his closing submissions, Mr Edwardson said the complainant's evidence was "bristling" with reasonable doubt.

He said the complainant had told AHPRA in 2023 that he had gone to see Mr Welch for a sexual health assessment, including an STI screening.

"When pressed [during evidence], it became obvious there was no testing for STIs," he said.

The complainant's cousin also gave evidence in court that he had told her about the incident shortly after it allegedly occurred.

Mr Edwardson highlighted in his closing statement that there were inconsistencies between their two statements: the cousin said the complainant was examined and grabbed under his underwear while standing, while the complainant said it was over his underwear.

Man's penis groped during ear piercing

The third charge of indecent assault related to when Mr Welch was piercing the second complainant's ear.

Mr Welch told the court he began providing professional piercing services in the early 2000s.

Mr Welch denied the allegation that when a part of the piercing fell into the man's lap, he groped the man's penis and testicles.

The matter will return to court in December, when Magistrate Jackie Hartnett is expected to hand down her findings.

World.title: Aussie star reaches WTA final as opponent says she was 'pressured' to withdraw
World.content:
Australian Talia Gibson has progressed to her first singles final on the main WTA tour at the expense of Tatiana Prozorova, who says she was "pressured" into withdrawing from their semifinal after failing part of a concussion test.

Gibson reached the final of the Singapore Open, where she will face a former grand slam finalist, as this year's French Open runner-up Maya Chwalinska and 2021 US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez face off in their final-four clash.

But 22-year-old Gibson was not required to step on court for her semi after receiving a walkover past Prozorova, who was hit by a smash during a doubles match.

The Russian stayed on the ground for some time before receiving a medical timeout and ultimately retiring from the match with partner Sofya Lansere, handing Australian Ellen Perez and Miyu Kato the victory.

But it later emerged, after Gibson's upset win over seventh seed Maria Sakkari in the quarterfinals, that Prozorova would not be able to line up in the final four.

The world number 180, who stunned popular Filipino third seed Alex Eala in the second round, said her "dream week came to an end" and she was clearly upset with the process.

On Instagram, Prozorova wrote that Kato's smash had mostly hit her shoulder and only "grazed" her cheek.

As she lay on the court, the umpire jumped from their chair and appeared to call for the physio, who Prozorova said "insisted" she leave the court for a medical timeout.

Tatiana Prozorova upset popular third seed Alex Eala earlier in the tournament. (Getty Images: Then Chih Wey/Xinhua)

"Unfortunately, I didn't know I could refuse," she wrote.

"The test wasn't easy. Given that I'd spent over three hours on court each of the last three days, I was fatigued and I struggled with some of the exercises — like standing on one leg with my eyes closed.

"To be honest, even when I'm fresh and well-rested, I find that difficult anyway. I explained this to the physio, too."

Prozorova said that one-legged test was the only aspect of the assessment she did not ace, but it was enough to rule her out.

"The physio also pressured me, implying I couldn't make my own decisions and needed at least six days (!!!) rest from tennis — which sounds crazy considering I was perfectly fine," she wrote.

Prozorova said she went through her usual recovery routine and "felt great" but the wheels were already in motion on the WTA's protocols.

"My team and I had a long discussion with the organisers; throughout the process, the physio pressured everyone present and even claimed I wasn't capable of taking responsibility for my own life," she wrote.

" The organisers' decision really upset me. My dream week came to an end today. "

She called on the WTA to "reconsider" the rules because the current system "renders players absolutely helpless".

If forced to sit out for six days, the 22-year-old will miss the chance to qualify for the China Open in Beijing, which starts on September 30.

"It is completely absurd and an overreach of authority by the WTA staff member," she wrote.

The WTA has been contacted for comment.

World.title: How the Dockers went from perpetual underdogs to top of the game
World.content:
It's a Dockers dream 32 years in the making — Fremantle are just one win away from premiership glory.

To their fans, the Dockers are the perpetual underdogs, a team that — according to historian Les Everett — was started to "dilute the West Coast Eagles".

Victorian clubs feared the Eagles were "getting too powerful" following their 1991 grand final appearance and premierships in 1992 and 1994.

There were many names put forward for Western Australia's second team, all with links to the port and sea, including the Pirates, Pelicans, Sharks, Dolphins and even the Doctors after Perth's famous sea breeze, the Fremantle Doctor.

The Dockers joined the competition in 1995, with futuristic purple footy shorts that were the "roomiest shorts in the AFL" compared to the tight fits of the 1980s.

Fremantle played their first AFL game in April 1995, taking on the Richmond Tigers at the MCG. (Supplied: Fremantle Football Club )

The purple origin

Coach Gerard Neesham paraded the team on the Fremantle Cappuccino Strip, telling reporters at the time "one of our briefs was to be innovative and we have definitely been that."

It was future thinking, with a nod to the past: the purple was inspired by the woollen hats historically worn by port workers, while the red and green colours on the kit came from the maritime signals for port and starboard.

The Dockers' identity is steeped in the maritime history of Fremantle and its dock workers, nicknamed wharfies. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

On the docks of Fremantle, wharfies still wear those purple beanies but in 2026, they have club logos.

As for the spirit of Wharfie Time, "it's passion, resilience and having that fight to never give up," said wharfie Jenson Chattaway.

"There will be tears if we win, I'll be crying for sure," added Port Services Officer Mike White.

Wharfies, including Jenson Chattaway (second from left) and Mike White (second from right), show their support for the Dockers. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Frustration forging greats

The early years were tough, with very little in the way of funding. The football club instead relied on 1000 donations of $1,000 each from their original fan group, the Harbour Masters.

Fremantle and West Coast quickly became fierce rivals. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: ALLSPORT/Tony McDonough)

But finally purple reigned in 1999. The club won its first game at the hallowed MCG and its first Western Derby, officially stepping out of the Eagles' shadow.

"In round 10, 1999, one of the Victorian newspapers said Melbourne only had to turn up to win the game at the MCG," historian Everett said.

"Fremantle played brilliantly, Tony Modra kicked 10 goals.

" The first derby win the same year was important, after losing the first nine to the Eagles, it was just a great relief really after being trapped as the little sibling to the Eagles. "

A year later, in 2000, Matthew Pavalich joined the Dockers. Through his career, he kicked 700 goals and as captain he took the team to its first decider in 2013.

Matthew Pavlich (centre) leads his teammates onto the MCG for the AFL grand final in 2013. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The famous all-rounder played alongside dual Brownlow Medal winner Nathan Fyfe. But it was not to be, and the Hawks shattered the Dockers' premiership dream by 15 points.

Fremantle lost to Hawthorn in the 2013 grand final. (AAP Image: David Crosling)

Daring to dream again

A new generation of players has taken the Dockers to the decider once again, and for Mr Everett, this is best team Fremantle has ever fielded.

Justin Longmuir's Dockers won the minor premiership and are now seeking their first flag. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"There is something about the way this team operates, there is a connection that makes it better than any team before," he said.

"It's been organically grown — it doesn't have any father-son gifts in it. Forged through good drafting, good trading, good development.

" That's been the story of Fremantle right from the start, it has been left to its own devices and if it wins the premiership it has done so itself. "

Even before the game began, the town was painted purple, and the team immortalised with a massive mural.

WA artist Jerome Davenport is painting the mural on the facade of Sailing for Oranges on the Cappuccino strip. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

But the players will achieve living legend status if they can take home the club's first ever premiership flag.

"If we do win it, I'll be watching the game again, again and again. I'll know every minute of it," Mr Everett said.

" Fremantle supporters, we've put ourselves through some misery, but I have never called myself a long-suffering Fremantle supporter, I have loved it. "

World.title: Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters Rob Harris September 26, 2026 — 10:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese has never been consumed by foreign affairs. He is not a student of geopolitics in the way some predecessors were. He does not appear particularly curious in the grand architecture of international relations. Albanese addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. Dominic Lorrimer But he does like making influential friends. He loves sitting down with other leaders, finding common ground or passions and building relationships that might be useful later. In a world where Australia has little capacity to impose its will, that is not nothing. And it is the foundation of Albanese’s middle-power strategy.



His week in New York has brought that into a sharper focus. He argued the international order is under great strain that superpowers are increasingly prepared to bend or ignore its rules, and that countries such as Australia need to work with other middle powers to stop the system collapsing into one governed by power alone. The political problem is that the more Albanese engages with the world, the more carefully he must explain why he is doing it. Albanese’s Global Citizen award at the Atlantic Council drew ridicule from his political opponents. Dominic Lorrimer There is a fine line between an Australian prime minister using international relationships to advance the national interest and one who appears to be spending too much time overseas while Australians are struggling with the cost of living. Albanese over the next few months he will travel to a G20 in Florida, potentially a Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, APEC in Shenzhen, a “G’day Namaste” event in Chennai plus COP Climate trips.



And waiting for him on the other side is One Nation’s Pauline Hanson, who understands something populists everywhere understand. That complicated problems are politically useful precisely because they can be made simple. Just look at her social media output this week. The UN has become a globalist plot. International agreements have become a surrender of sovereignty and climate pacts are men in suits in far-off lands telling Australians how to live. The government’s efforts to tackle the algorithm are now a plot to curb speech and political association. You do not need to engage in nuance. You ask why the prime minister is in New York when people at home are struggling to pay their bills? That is the populist challenge Albanese and many of his fellow leaders across the West, in particular, face. Albanese cannot defeat it merely by saying the UN is important. He will have to explain why it matters to Australians.



There’s no doubt that the international order was never perfect, but for decades it provided a framework in which countries could at least argue about the rules. It has ensured relative peace and held the world back from the brink on more than one occasion. Related Article United Nations Ignored, mocked, harangued – what’s the point of the UN any more? Russia shattered the principle of territorial sovereignty in Europe in 2014 when it annexed Crimea and – with next to no consequence – went back for more in 2022. China and the United States are locked in strategic competition. Donald Trump’s America has shown diminishing patience with many of the institutions and alliances that underpinned the postwar system. Beijing’s assertiveness in our backyard frightens the hell out of many. Trump’s war in the Middle East sent our fuel prices higher and trade wars have hit Australian exporters and consumers.



The revelation of an AI agent gaining access to an Australian government Medicare system gave the argument an immediate local dimension. Suddenly, an esoteric debate about AI safety had found its way into one of the most familiar institutions in Australian life. This is where Albanese’s international agenda has substance. He was not simply collecting selfies for his Instagram, he was trying to build co-operation around problems that will eventually land on Australian soil. But the substance is not enough, he must prosecute the case again and again. That has sometimes been Albanese’s weakness. He spends months building a policy or diplomatic initiative and then muddles the moment it arrives. A critic will find a simpler line and the government ends up explaining itself rather than making the case. Hanson does not need to win the argument about the UN in all its complexity. She needs to make Australians feel Albanese is worrying about the wrong things.



Inflation and increased economic insecurity has ensured there’s already a constituency asking why the prime minister is travelling so much. Why he is meeting foreign leaders? Why taxpayers should care about an institution in New York when household budgets are under pressure? They are not inherently unreasonable questions but the danger is allowing the answers to be dictated by the lowest common denominator. The world comes home whether Australians are interested in it or not. Jobs depend on trade. National security depends on alliances and diplomacy. AI will change Australian workplaces. That is the case Albanese needs to make. And he will need to make it with greater conviction. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Ivan Cleary declares Nathan Cleary fit to take on Knights in prelim final
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Ivan Cleary declares Nathan Cleary fit to take on Knights in prelim final Adrian Proszenko September 26, 2026 — 10:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith coach Ivan Cleary has declared son and champion halfback Nathan a certain starter for Sunday’s preliminary final against Newcastle. Nathan Cleary is recovering from a stress-related bone issue in his right kicking foot, an injury he suffered in the qualifying final win against the Roosters. Nathan Cleary at Panthers training this week. Wolter Peeters The Panthers co-captain trained without incident on Friday night. The club has attempted to prevent the media this week from obtaining images of Cleary training by plastering tarpaulin around the club’s training base. “He’s going well, definitely handy to have that week off there. So he’s good,” Ivan Cleary said of Nathan during his pre-game press conference on Saturday.



“He’s done the work, so looking forward to seeing him out there.” Jack Cole has been named to partner Nathan Cleary in the halves, despite Jack Cogger - named on an extended bench - being available after serving a suspension. Ivan Cleary ruled out the prospect of his son starting off the bench. Penrith coach Ivan Cleary says son Nathan is fit to take on the Knights in the preliminary final. Audrey Richardson “No, Nat’s ready to play,” he said. “He’s obviously carrying an injury, but there wouldn’t be many players out there at the moment for any team that aren’t. It’s just that time of year, but we’re super confident that all our players are ready to play.” Cleary said it was too early to determine whether Nathan would be fit for Australia selection for the season-ending Rugby League World Cup. He added there was a chance the halfback’s foot was fractured, but MRI scans are often inconclusive.



“There’s basically enough on there that there’s something wrong,” he said. “But to you’ve got to go by what I think is called ‘clinically’ - how does it feel, can you walk, etc. So we’ve basically worked out enough that it’s an injury that could get worse, for sure, so we’re trying to manage it as best we can so he can play so we can get him to play … Loading “He’ll be ready. Yeah, he’s done a bit of everything. He’s actually living with us at the moment, so I’ve actually seen firsthand how much he’s actually done. It’s crazy, yeah. He has left no stone unturned.” Sam Walker played through the pain of a syndesmosis injury that required surgery less than a month ago in the Roosters’ preliminary final win against the Dolphins on Friday night.



“This is what the players dream about,” Cleary said. “It’s what they go through all the hard work in pre-season for, and all through the year, to get themselves into this sort of arena. So, they’re all true competitors and they find ways to get out there and perform.” Cleary paid tribute to the Penrith medical staff who had made a slew of stars available for big games. Fullback Dylan Edwards was nursed through a serious foot injury in the 2021 finals series, while Nathan Cleary and Isaah Yeo (pectoral) have defied the odds to figure in the 2026 play-off campaign. Isaah Yeo has made a remarkable recovery from a pec injury. Panthers Digital “The medical team’s amazing,” Cleary said. “Their job is way more than just treating people - there’s a lot of decisions to make, even like reading scans and trying to work out what’s the best course of action. “It’s not like a normal person where you treat them with the utmost care; you’re sort of trying to throw them out on a footy field as well if you can. It’s pretty cool to see how it all works. We’ve got good chemistry through our staff, and we’ve been together for a fairly long time, so I think that helps as well.”



Related Article NRL 2026 Kalyn Ponga wasn’t ready to lead the Knights in 2022. He is now Cleary said a 25-6 loss to Newcastle at Carrington Park in Bathurst last May - a result that consigned the Panthers to last place at the time - was a pivotal moment. “Oh, that was awful, that game,” he said. “That was our turning point last year, because it was sort of the day where we just went, ‘right, this is not good enough. We are what we are, and it’s not very good.’ “So it was cool. I mean, the Knights, they’ve been amazing. They are an absolute threat.



“They’ve got a team that’s overcome a lot of things this year. They’ve got a young team with a lot of players on the way up and having the best seasons of their lives. They’ve got amazing support behind them. They haven’t had a lot of success over the last period of time, so that’s cool for them. An amazing footy fraternity up there, and it’s good to see them back in the big games.” Cleary made light of the tarpaulin used to block out prying eyes, a tactic the club normally only employs for grand final week. “We’re just trying to prepare in peace. Someone was snapping a few things behind the scenes the other day,” Cleary quipped. “Preparation is very important for us. No one wants to go see a dress rehearsal, do they? The show’s on tomorrow, so you can all see it then.”

World.title: U2 rock their old school with surprise concert to mark 50 years
World.content:
WorldEuropeIreland U2 rock their old school with surprise concert to mark 50 years David Crowe September 26, 2026 — 10:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Irish rock group U2 have gone back to school to perform to students and teachers on the grounds where they formed their band 50 years ago. The group followed the school performance with a surprise concert on a Dublin pedestrian mall famous for hosting buskers, where they played from a building as hundreds of fans gathered below. U2 have celebrated their 50th Anniversary by returning to Mount Temple Comprehensive School. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for U2 Lead singer Bono joked to Irish national broadcaster RTE that the band’s lead guitarist, The Edge, was worried the students at their old school, Mount Temple Comprehensive, might not have liked the band. “But they can’t ask for their money back,” the singer said. “Because it’s free.”



U2 formed at the school when the band’s drummer, Larry Mullen Jnr, posted a note on a school notice board asking if fellow students wanted to join a band. Their Friday concert on the school grounds was held 50 years to the day after the band members first gathered at Mullen’s family home in Dublin on September 25, 1976. They performed at the same school building where they were photographed in 1977 in their first iteration as a band, three years before they released their first album, Boy. At their Friday concert they performed their first hit from that album, I Will Follow. The Edge joked about the contrast between the Friday concert and their debut on the school grounds.



“I think we were good. I think the sound was better this time, is my sense, and I was more in tune,” he told RTE. U2 in 1979: from left, Adam Clayton, Larry Mullen Jr., David Evans (aka “the Edge”) and Bono. Paul Slattery The band performed hits including Vertigo, Beautiful Day and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio. The band finished the school performance with a rendition of their hit, One, with backing from music students playing violins, cellos and harps. The band are considered one of the world’s biggest rock groups with an estimated 170 million record sales, placing them 22nd on a Wikipedia list of major artists by sales volume. (The Beatles rank first with 600 million sales; Australia’s biggest musical export, AC/DC, have an estimated 200 million sales.)



Bono looks out on the crowd as U2 perform an impromptu concert from a balcony in central Dublin, Ireland. AP Photo/Peter Morrison A few hours after the school concert, crowds gathered in Grafton Street – one of Dublin’s main pedestrian thoroughfares – as rumours circulated about a free concert. The band appeared on the first-floor balcony if a Dublin landmark, Bewley’s Café, and began a concert for hundreds of people gathered in the street below. Crowd lapping up the impromptu concert from U2 in Grafton Street – one of Dublin’s main pedestrian thoroughfares. AP Photo/Peter Morrison They performed I Will Follow as well as another song from their earliest days, Out of Control. They also performed One, Where the Streets Have No Name, Silencio and With or Without You.



Related Article Live music ‘We weren’t the next big thing’: Irish singer-songwriter’s unusual path to success The Grafton Street concert also included a moment to honour the Irish songwriter Glen Hansard, who died in July. He was a regular busker in the Dublin street before the global success of the film Once, which featured songs he wrote and performed with Markéta Irglová. U2 performed Falling Slowly, one of the songs from the film. Hansard, who died in July, had a long association with Grafton Street and was closely associated with the annual Christmas Eve charity busk in Dublin city centre. The band’s next album, Carnaval de Luz, is due to be released in November and includes a track co-written and performed with Dolly Parton, the American music star who died last month. World.title: Learn from ‘extraordinary figures in Australian food’ at Powerhouse Parramatta launch
World.content:
Eating outRestaurant news Learn from ‘extraordinary figures in Australian food’ at Powerhouse Parramatta launch There’s a Maggie Beer talk, a fish butchery demo by Saint Peter chef Josh Niland, sit-down Lebanese feasts with Sunday Kitchen and more. Bianca Hrovat September 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Josh Niland, Maggie Beer and Stephanie Alexander are among the celebrated chefs and food personalities scheduled to appear at Powerhouse Parramatta during its 23-day opening festival, commencing November 7. Food will play a central role at the $915 million western Sydney institution, which will kick off its first in-house food program with a series of cooking demonstrations, dinners and discussions ranging from $15 to $50 a ticket. Stephanie Alexander in front of Powerhouse Parramatta. Andy Roberts “The opening festival feels deeply aligned with what Powerhouse Parramatta aspires to be – a place where culture is not simply presented to audiences, but made with, by and for communities,” says Powerhouse Parramatta associate Kylie Kwong. “Coming from a Chinese extended family, I feel a personal connection to the multicultural communities of western Sydney and an understanding of the ways food carries family history, identity and belonging across generations.”



The museum has spent years preparing for this moment, having appointed Kwong as an associate in 2024. Together with a dedicated food team, the chef assisted in building ties within the local food community, curating sold-out events to showcase businesses such as Harris Park restaurant IndoChainese and Australia’s largest insect protein farm, Circle Harvest. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Family DINEasties is one of the sold out events at Powerhouse Parramatta’s opening festival, (left to right) Patrick La, Chea Sreng, Ny Chan, Lang Sreng, Kevin La, Poi La and Jeffrey La, of Sengtavanh Asian Grocery. Nikki To That investment paid off this week when three of the food program’s inaugural events sold out within days: the Family DINEasties feast hosted by Kwong with writers Lee Tran Lam and Kevin La, presented in collaboration with the SBS Food show of the same name. “The festival ... brings together extraordinary figures in Australian food,” says Kwong. Three-hatted Saint Peter chef Josh Niland will share his pioneering scale-to-tail seafood philosophy, and leading figures featured in the Powerhouse’s Australian Culinary Archive – including Maggie Beer, Neil Perry and Good Food Guide Bill Granger Trailblazer award recipient Sharon Winsor – will gather on November 9 to tell the stories that have shaped Australia’s food culture.



Other standout events (with tickets still available at the time of publication) include demonstrations from Chat Thai restaurateur Palisa Anderson and Hai Au Lang Nuong (Canley Vale) owner-chef Ben Nguyen. Josh Niland in Fish Butchery Waterloo. Steven Siewert “[Food] is super democratic – it brings in these people, like cooks or entrepreneurs or researchers, who are not traditionally involved in museum programming per se, but they contribute so much to the arts and sciences,” says Powerhouse Parramatta producer Cheyenne Bardos. Events will be held throughout the new building, which took more than four years to construct and houses a working rooftop garden led by the Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Foundation, a full commercial kitchen and a 200-seat amphitheatre demonstration kitchen. Simon Sandall, owner-chef of Gladesville restaurant Boronia Kitchen, will take over the in-house restaurant, with a new but yet-to-be-named culinary venture from the owner-chef.



Kylie Kwong at Chatkazz restaurant in Harris Park. Louise Kennerley “We want people to be able to come to the food program and see themselves and their work reflected in that, whether it’s their culture or the things they like to eat or the way they like to come together through food,” says Bardos. “There’s so much depth and richness and complexity there.” Powerhouse Parramatta opens to the public on Saturday, November 7. Its opening festival will include 179 events, 65 per cent of which are free-of-charge, spanning from First Nations culture to space and science. The full program and tickets are available at powerhouse.com.au.

World.title: ‘That’s just Nestor’: The ridiculous thing about Irankunda’s Brazil wondergoal
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer ‘That’s just Nestor’: The ridiculous thing about Irankunda’s Brazil wondergoal Vince Rugari September 26, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nestory Irankunda’s goal against Brazil was audacious, breathtaking and utterly ridiculous. It was also entirely predictable. “It’s almost funny,” Jackson Irvine said. “You just laugh because it’s just like, yeah, of course he does. Of course he did. That’s just Nestor.” Loading Irankunda’s wicked, drifting strike from well outside the box deserved to be the matchwinner on Friday night - and it very nearly was, until Rayan’s header deep in stoppage time salvaged a 1-1 draw for the five-time world champions in a friendly in Townsville.



The late equaliser robbed Australia of what would have been just their second victory over Brazil - but Irankunda’s goal was the second time a Socceroos player has scored against them, which means it should go down in history regardless. When Paul Okon jnr drew a foul a few metres out from the edge of the penalty area, Irankunda’s eyes lit up. He has scored plenty of direct free kicks at club level, but hitherto none in a Socceroos jersey. Here was his chance, positioned perfectly within his range. Nestory Irankunda. Getty Images “You know something special can happen when the ball’s at his feet,” said defender Aziz Behich. Brazil’s legendary coach, Carlo Ancelotti, knew it, too.



“We knew he was a fantastic player,” he said. “He’s a player with a lot of talent. He’s doing really well in Europe. We knew [what he could do in] this kind of situation, on set pieces. He shot fantastic.” Remember: Irankunda is only 20 years old, which means Socceroos fans can look forward to at least another decade of watching him play; of knowing that so long he is on the field, Australia is a chance of winning any game, because he can produce magic like that out of nowhere. Tony Popovic with Nestory Irankunda on Friday night. Getty Images On a night built around Brazil’s array of superstars - Vinicius jnr, Raphinha, Bruno Guimaraes et al - Irankunda stole the spotlight, giving the 25,000 fans at Queensland Country Bank Stadium a ‘where were you?’ story they can dine out on for years, and for the many budding young footballers in the crowd, a flash of inspiration they could take home. Earlier in the week, Irankunda had spoken of his desire to build a career with the Socceroos that would “be remembered”. Moments like this are how that happens, and the significance of it was not lost on him.



“People see that and they keep talking about it for a while,” Irankunda said. “We’ve got the main sports here in Australia, which is the NRL and the AFL. I feel like football is very underrated here. What we’ve done at the World Cup and what we’re doing now, it’s something new. It’s the new generation, the next generation. Nestory Irankunda celebrates after scoring against Brazil. Getty Images “It feels great to play against the world’s best, and to score against them felt great. It just shows that we can play football as well. I’ve said this multiple times: Australia has the talent. We’ve just got to find a way to show that.” Coach Tony Popovic said he could see a “clear difference” in Irankunda since the World Cup, where he started three games and came off the bench in another, scoring another cracker in Australia’s famous win over Turkey.



His performances earned him a $25 million transfer to Portuguese giants Sporting Lisbon, where he is still trying to establish himself as a starting player. That battle continues, but Popovic said he could see a significant change in his maturity since the move, declaring his development was “well ahead” of what he expected from him at this point in his career. “What he’s learning is that the transfer is one part. Now you go to a new club, they don’t give you minutes, they don’t guarantee you minutes, they give you nothing. You have to earn everything,” Popovic said. “That’s what we want at the Socceroos. Names don’t just get a starting spot. He delivered today, played very well and he’ll only get better. “You can just imagine when he’s 24 or 28, if he can stay fit and play and play and play, and just keep getting better physically, and now he’s understanding the game ... Sporting is doing a good job with him, tactically helping him understand a lot of situations on the field that are non-negotiable. A lot of that is work rate, a lot of that is getting in position and he’s understanding that. It’s just normal. It’s evolution.”



Related Article Friendlies Socceroos v Brazil as it happened: Brazil equalise in final seconds after Irankunda’s stunner put Australia in the lead Popovic copped major criticism for deploying Irankunda at striker during the World Cup, instead of his natural position on the wing, where he played against Brazil. Out wide, he looks far more free to express himself; in just the seventh minute, he went on one of his typical nitro-boost runs down the left flank, before cutting inside and forcing a terrific reaction save by Hugo Souza from distance. When he gets going, he’s almost impossible to stop, but it’s difficult to get the room to do things like that centrally. “To be able to hit one in the first half on the run at full speed ... that technique is so difficult,” said Irvine. “[But] from a dead ball, he’s just lethal.” While many fans and pundits remain unsure about Popovic’s tenure, and whether he should be retained beyond January’s Asian Cup, what’s clear is that Irankunda appreciates the tough love he has shown him, and he would run through a brick wall for him in return.



“To be honest, he deserves the credit,” Irankunda said. “He’s pushed me and he’s trying to help me become a better player ... sometimes he’s hard on me, which is fine with me, as long as I know that he has good intentions.”

World.title: Thirty years on from their maiden World Cup, the Springboks are a team for all South Africans
World.content:
SportRugby UnionSouth Africa rugby Thirty years on from their maiden World Cup, the Springboks are a team for all South Africans Jonathan Drennan September 26, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Springboks’ bench named to face the Wallabies in Perth on Sunday night is largely defined by its ability to change a game at will. It has eight world-class players who have the potential to dominate fatigued opponents with both speed and strength. Those players also tell the story of the modern South Africa they represent. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu taking on the Wallabies in 2024 Getty Images Back-rower Jasper Wiese grew up on a remote Northern Cape farm, his junior school too small to field a rugby team. Prop Ox Nche was born in the Free State town of Thaba ’Nchu, where organised sport was a luxury few could access. Playmaker Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu was born in Cape Town to Nick Feinberg, the son of a white anti-apartheid campaigner, and Makhosazana Mngomezulu, a lawyer of Zulu descent.



Every player who represents the Springboks carries the legacy of the 1995 World Cup final win. That victory gave a glimpse into what was possible for South Africa as a society, but also highlighted the huge amount of work still to do in a country that had recently emerged from the horrors of apartheid. Morne du Plessis is one of South African rugby’s greatest captains, leading the Springboks to 13 wins in 15 Tests from 1975 to 1980. But one of his greatest achievements was as team manager for the 1995 champions. South African rugby captain Francois Pienaar after the 1995 World Cup final. AP He was able to see both sides of South African rugby – the one that was closed to the majority of the country and the one that started to open up. “Before ’95, we were deeply divided [as a country]; a minority of people would support the Springboks in those years that I played, and let’s be frank about that,” du Plessis said.



“And the World Cup win of ’95, I’d like to believe, was a catalyst for change. Mandela, himself agreeing to continue with the Springbok emblem and the Springbok jersey, was pivotal as well. “Mandela had the foresight that rugby, being what it was and where it came from, could be a catalyst in pulling people together.” Rassie Erasmus has led the Springboks to two World Cup victories, but also helped transform support for the team. Getty Images The South Africa side that beat New Zealand in the 1995 final contained only one non-white player: the late Chester Williams, who started on the left wing. Du Plessis knew more work needed to be done before the Springboks would be embraced by the entire nation. He has watched as the momentum lost after 1995 was regained with the emergence of coach Rassie Erasmus, his captain Siya Kolisi and an all-conquering team.



“I played in the apartheid days, and I was the manager in ’95, so I saw both sides. I was privileged to see the new dawn, as it were,” Du Plessis said. “From then on, it lost a little bit of momentum because there weren’t standout opportunities again like that. But then came Rassie and Siya, and they’ve taken that unifying ability of rugby to another level. Absolutely another level.” South Africa fans at the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France. Getty Erasmus grew up in the working-class Eastern Cape town of Despatch, completing his compulsory military service in 1991. That same year, Kolisi was born in the Port Elizabeth township of Zwide. They came from entirely different worlds, but in 2018 Erasmus named Kolisi as the first black captain of the Springboks, a move that helped the team attract widespread support. Many black players selected in the Test after 1995 were unfairly scrutinised, in some cases being made to feel unwelcome. But the appointment of Kolisi as captain by Erasmus, a former Afrikaner Springbok, carried huge weight and opened the eyes of many non-white South Africans to possibilities in the game they hadn’t previously imagined.



“For many years, transformation – meaning giving everybody a fair chance of coming through the system and making it to the top – was seen by many people, whether they’d admit it or not, as a sort of punishment, a payback, something we have to go through for a while,” rugby commentator John Robbie said. “There was this dreadful phrase of ‘quota players’, where you had guys who many from the white community [in South Africa] said were not good enough and the [non-white] players themselves would say, ‘no one takes us seriously.’ Loading “That doesn’t happen any more ... what Rassie has done is seen beyond that prism of biases. He’s seen this massive number of people, the potential in a community that never got the chance before. And the answer is what we see on the field.” If you drive through South Africa, you get an idea of the power of the Springboks and how the whole country embraces them as a team. Winning two World Cups in a row, of course, helps, but representation helps the support to endure. In the townships, the suburbs, the city centres and throughout farmland, you see Springbok jerseys.



Bob Skinstad played 42 times for South Africa and was part of the 2007 World Cup-winning squad. He made his Test debut in 1997 and competed directly with Erasmus as a player, before watching him take the team to World Cup wins in 2019 and 2023. Skinstad sees the impact of Kolisi’s leadership of the Springboks within his own family; the back-rower has become a hero to the nation. Siya Kolisi with fans in South Africa. AP “My young 12-year-old son doesn’t want to be Bob Skinstad, he wants to be Siya Kolisi and many years ago that wouldn’t have been true, because there would have been a racial divide between what children wanted to be,” Skinstad said. “If you look at the transformation of the team, they represent all corners of South Africa. It’s been something that everybody’s been able to get behind, and something that South Africans are really proud of.”



Related Article Updated

Wallabies Suaalii named on wing as Wallabies stack bench to combat Springboks’ bomb squad Skinstad’s work as a business consultant and an investor in Beziers rugby club in France takes him all over the world. He witnessed the huge crowds that followed the Springboks to watch them defeat New Zealand in Baltimore recently. On Sunday, thousands more South Africans will gather in Perth to cheer on a team that gives them an impenetrable link to their home country. “We feel very privileged that we’ve got a number of quality individuals who are willing to represent South Africa and go out there and put their bodies on the line for what is essentially a cause that’s bigger than themselves. It’s a cause for the country. It’s not just a cause for the team,” Skinstad said. “Wherever you are around the world, that national team means much more than just the results on the field. It means a link back to your home country and probably the place of your birth, and family and friends, and a whole bunch of other emotional ties.”



South Africa’s problems will never be solved entirely by a unified rugby team. This month, the bodies of nine women were found in South Africa’s Ekurhuleni municipality, forcing Kolisi to post on Instagram ahead of the Wallabies Test, stating, “violence against women is an everyday reality in our country, and we cannot keep leaving women to carry this fight alone. I don’t have all the answers. But silence is not an option. Awareness is not enough. We need action.” Related Article Wallabies ‘I knew we had that belief’: How the Wallabies broke their 62-year Ellis Park curse No other Test rugby captain carries such responsibility to not only lead a team on the field, but also a country off it. Crime, violence, governance issues and unemployment remain realities for many in South Africa, but the world champion Springboks provide a glimpse of what is possible when all strands of its 64 million population, with 12 official languages and diverse cultures, combine.

World.title: The Knights declared Tom Jenkins would be a ‘long-term NRL player’. They were half right
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Knights declared Tom Jenkins would be a ‘long-term NRL player’. They were half right Christian Nicolussi September 26, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Newcastle Knights’ official press release in October 2023 declared Tom Jenkins was someone they believed would be a “long-term NRL player”. The Knights were half right: Jenkins has gone on to become a mainstay in the NRL – at a rival club. Tom Jenkins on debut for Newcastle in 2024. NRL Photos Penrith and Jenkins will run out at Accor Stadium on Sunday afternoon against the club he signed with just three years ago. The 25-year-old Jenkins will even be on the same side of the field as Knights centre Dane Gagai, the veteran who taught him plenty of lessons during his short stay in the Hunter.



Jenkins remembers making his club debut for the Knights in round two of the 2024 season. Former coach Adam O’Brien casually yelled out the good news while Jenkins was in the bathroom. Jack Cogger, who has also since returned to Penrith, handed him his Knights jersey. They played against North Queensland, the club that had offered Jenkins a two-year deal. Penrith flyer Tom Jenkins has been excellent this year with 30 tries. Wolter Peeters So how is it a winger who has scored tries for fun at Penrith, and is just 160 minutes away from his first premiership ring, scraped together just five games at Newcastle? “I had all intentions of being a long-term first-grader, and being a long-term first-grader for Newcastle,” Jenkins said.



“I was roomies with ‘Cogs’ [Cogger]. He gave me my club debut jersey, which was a nice memory. All the boys were great up there, and they enjoyed a laugh. “The biggest one for me was ‘Gags’ [Gagai]. He’s such a talented player and I have so much respect for him. He kept telling me to stick to what I’m good at, and to keep backing myself. Thomas Jenkins has been a revelation for Penrith this year. Getty Images “I just wasn’t the right fit for them, and they weren’t the right fit for me. That became pretty obvious. “I wasn’t getting what I needed as a player from the coach, and he [O’Brien] wasn’t getting the performances from me as a player.



“I needed a change. If I wasn’t going to be playing good footy, I might as well have been back here doing what I enjoy.” Jenkins grew up in Boorowa, about 90 minutes north of Canberra, and started his NRL career at the Panthers. He made his debut in the NRL in the final round of 2022, in Townsville, and his fondest memory is Eddie Blacker chasing down Scott Drinkwater (“make sure you put that in because Eddie will love it.“) Related Article NRL 2026 Dropped, departing and dangerous: The Origin axing that lit a fire under Brian To’o When the chance to play more regular football in Newcastle did not eventuate, he was prepared to play Ron Massey Cup with St Marys, while making sure Penrith coach Ivan Cleary knew he was back in the neighbourhood. The more football Jenkins has played, the more he has grown in confidence, which has led to him being more vocal – almost annoying, according to some – around the group.



“He speaks really well in front of the cameras, but he’s the foghorn and extravert inside our four walls,” co-captain Isaah Yeo said. “He’s been outstanding for us, he’s brought a real confidence, and you can see that in the way he plays. He’s hard to tackle, super confident in the air, and while everyone sees the tries he scores [30 in 25 games], defensively, in our system, he’s been exceptional. I’m so happy with the way he’s played.”

World.title: Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters Rob Harris September 26, 2026 — 10:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese has never been consumed by foreign affairs. He is not a student of geopolitics in the way some predecessors were. He does not appear particularly curious in the grand architecture of international relations. Albanese addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. Dominic Lorrimer But he does like making influential friends. He loves sitting down with other leaders, finding common ground or passions and building relationships that might be useful later. In a world where Australia has little capacity to impose its will, that is not nothing. And it is the foundation of Albanese’s middle-power strategy.



His week in New York has brought that into a sharper focus. He argued the international order is under great strain that superpowers are increasingly prepared to bend or ignore its rules, and that countries such as Australia need to work with other middle powers to stop the system collapsing into one governed by power alone. The political problem is that the more Albanese engages with the world, the more carefully he must explain why he is doing it. Albanese’s Global Citizen award at the Atlantic Council drew ridicule from his political opponents. Dominic Lorrimer There is a fine line between an Australian prime minister using international relationships to advance the national interest and one who appears to be spending too much time overseas while Australians are struggling with the cost of living. Albanese over the next few months he will travel to a G20 in Florida, potentially a Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, APEC in Shenzhen, a “G’day Namaste” event in Chennai plus COP Climate trips.



And waiting for him on the other side is One Nation’s Pauline Hanson, who understands something populists everywhere understand. That complicated problems are politically useful precisely because they can be made simple. Just look at her social media output this week. The UN has become a globalist plot. International agreements have become a surrender of sovereignty and climate pacts are men in suits in far-off lands telling Australians how to live. The government’s efforts to tackle the algorithm are now a plot to curb speech and political association. You do not need to engage in nuance. You ask why the prime minister is in New York when people at home are struggling to pay their bills? That is the populist challenge Albanese and many of his fellow leaders across the West, in particular, face. Albanese cannot defeat it merely by saying the UN is important. He will have to explain why it matters to Australians.



There’s no doubt that the international order was never perfect, but for decades it provided a framework in which countries could at least argue about the rules. It has ensured relative peace and held the world back from the brink on more than one occasion. Related Article United Nations Ignored, mocked, harangued – what’s the point of the UN any more? Russia shattered the principle of territorial sovereignty in Europe in 2014 when it annexed Crimea and – with next to no consequence – went back for more in 2022. China and the United States are locked in strategic competition. Donald Trump’s America has shown diminishing patience with many of the institutions and alliances that underpinned the postwar system. Beijing’s assertiveness in our backyard frightens the hell out of many. Trump’s war in the Middle East sent our fuel prices higher and trade wars have hit Australian exporters and consumers.



The revelation of an AI agent gaining access to an Australian government Medicare system gave the argument an immediate local dimension. Suddenly, an esoteric debate about AI safety had found its way into one of the most familiar institutions in Australian life. This is where Albanese’s international agenda has substance. He was not simply collecting selfies for his Instagram, he was trying to build co-operation around problems that will eventually land on Australian soil. But the substance is not enough, he must prosecute the case again and again. That has sometimes been Albanese’s weakness. He spends months building a policy or diplomatic initiative and then muddles the moment it arrives. A critic will find a simpler line and the government ends up explaining itself rather than making the case. Hanson does not need to win the argument about the UN in all its complexity. She needs to make Australians feel Albanese is worrying about the wrong things.



Inflation and increased economic insecurity has ensured there’s already a constituency asking why the prime minister is travelling so much. Why he is meeting foreign leaders? Why taxpayers should care about an institution in New York when household budgets are under pressure? They are not inherently unreasonable questions but the danger is allowing the answers to be dictated by the lowest common denominator. The world comes home whether Australians are interested in it or not. Jobs depend on trade. National security depends on alliances and diplomacy. AI will change Australian workplaces. That is the case Albanese needs to make. And he will need to make it with greater conviction. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
